Adoniram Byfield.bio: Son of the preacher Nicholas Byfield, and one of the two scribes of the Westminster Assembly. That office is why his name survives: it stands on the printed Directory for Public Worship and on other Assembly papers, certifying them as the Assembly's own act. He had served earlier as a chaplain to a parliamentary regiment, and held country livings, ending at Collingbourne Ducis in Wiltshire. He published almost nothing under his own name. A reader meets him as the hand behind the documents rather than as a divine with a body of work.

Albert the Great.affiliation: Master of theology at Paris; Bishop of Regensburg, 1260–1262
Albert the Great.bio: Albertus Magnus, the Dominican who set out to make the whole of Aristotle available to Latin readers, paraphrasing and expanding the logical, physical, ethical and metaphysical works and adding his own observation in De animalibus and De vegetabilibus. He taught at Paris and then founded the Dominican studium at Cologne, where Thomas Aquinas was his student. He served as provincial of the German province and briefly as bishop of Regensburg before returning to teaching. Canonized in 1931 and named a Doctor of the Church, he is read for the joining of natural inquiry to theology.

Aldo Landi.bio: Italian historian of the conciliar movement. He is read here for Il papa deposto (Pisa 1409), a study of the council that deposed both claimants in the Great Schism and of the conciliar ideas that made such a deposition arguable in canon law. Readers meeting him beside the conciliar acta will find him a guide to how the fifteenth century reasoned about a council judging a pope, rather than a primary voice of the period.

Alfonso Salmerón.affiliation: Papal theologian at the Council of Trent
Alfonso Salmerón.bio: One of the first companions of Ignatius Loyola, gathered at Paris while a student there after early work at Alcalá. He was sent as a papal theologian to the Council of Trent and spoke in all three of its periods, an unusual continuity across nearly twenty years of council. He was used on missions to Ireland, Poland and Germany, and led the Jesuit province and college at Naples. His sixteen volumes of commentaries on the Gospels, Acts and the Epistles were published after his death and represent Jesuit exegesis in its first generation.

Alonso Tostado.bio: Alfonso Fernández de Madrigal, called El Tostado, a Salamanca master whose output became proverbial for size: commentaries on the historical books of the Old Testament and on Matthew that fill twenty-seven folio volumes. Propositions of his on confession and satisfaction were challenged before Eugenius IV in 1443 and answered by Juan de Torquemada, an exchange that placed him among those pressing the limits of papal authority in the decades after Basel. He was made bishop of Ávila in 1449 and died six years later. He is read for the scale and literalism of his exegesis.

Andreas Essenius.bio: Dutch Reformed theologian and colleague of Gisbertus Voetius at Utrecht, where he taught dogmatics and practical divinity. His Systema theologicum and the shorter compendium drawn from it belong to the settled scholastic phase of Dutch Reformed teaching. He is met most often as a controversialist: against Roman Catholic opponents, and above all against the Cartesian theology of Christoph Wittich, whom he charged with letting philosophy dictate how Scripture may be read. Readers working on the Dutch quarrel over Descartes will find him on the Voetian side of nearly every exchange.

Andreas Hyperius.bio: Born at Ypres, from which the name, and educated at Paris and Louvain before several years of study in England. From 1542 he taught theology at Marburg. His De formandis concionibus sacris (1553) is the first Protestant textbook of preaching, sorting sermons by their ends and giving the Reformed pulpit a method it used for a century. The Methodi theologiae did comparable work for the ordering of doctrine, and De publica in pauperes beneficentia argued the case for organized civic poor relief. He is read as the man who turned Reformation preaching into a teachable discipline.

Andrew Perne.bio: Two English clergymen carry this name, and the context of the collection decides which is meant. Andrew Perne of Wilby in Northamptonshire, who died in 1654, was a member of the Westminster Assembly and preached fast sermons before the Long Parliament; his published work is small. The elder Andrew Perne, c. 1519 to 1589, was Master of Peterhouse and Dean of Ely, repeatedly vice-chancellor of Cambridge, remembered for conforming under four successive religious settlements and for what he gave to the university library. Nothing here should be transferred from one to the other.

Anthony Tuckney.affiliation: Master of Emmanuel and of St John's College, Cambridge; Regius Professor of Divinity
Anthony Tuckney.bio: Succeeded John Cotton at Boston in Lincolnshire, then sat in the Westminster Assembly, where he was among the hands most active in framing the Shorter Catechism. He was made Master of Emmanuel College in 1645, Master of St John's in 1653, and Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge in 1655, and was removed after the Restoration. His correspondence with Benjamin Whichcote, printed long afterward, is the classic exchange between Puritan divinity and the Cambridge Platonists over reason, grace and the language of theology. His Praelectiones theologicae appeared posthumously.

Antoine Arnauld.bio: The youngest of the Arnauld family and the intellectual center of Port-Royal, known as le grand Arnauld. De la fréquente communion (1643) attacked what he took to be lax Jesuit practice in confession and communion. His defense of Jansenius brought his expulsion from the Sorbonne in 1656, the occasion of Pascal's Provincial Letters. With Pierre Nicole he wrote the Port-Royal Logic, and with Claude Lancelot the Grammaire générale; with Malebranche he disputed at length over ideas and over grace. His last years were spent in exile in the Low Countries.

Antonio Possevino.bio: Jesuit diplomat employed by Gregory XIII in the most exposed negotiations of the period: a mission to Sweden aimed at John III, work in Poland, and the mediation between Ivan IV of Muscovy and Stephen Báthory that produced the truce of 1582. His Moscovia reported what he had seen of Russian religion and government to a Western readership that had little else. In later life he turned to reference work, compiling the Bibliotheca selecta and the Apparatus sacer, guides to what a Catholic scholar should read, and what he should not.

August Franzen & Wolfgang Müller (Hrsg.).bio: Named here as editors, Hrsg. being the German abbreviation for that role, rather than as authors. August Franzen taught church history at Freiburg and Bonn and wrote a Kleine Kirchengeschichte that served generations of students. With Wolfgang Müller he edited a collected volume of essays on the history and theology of the Council of Constance, published at Freiburg in the 1960s. What stands behind the entry is a gathering of specialist studies by many hands, not a single continuous argument.

Bartholomew de Barberiis.bio: The Latinized form of the name points to an early modern Catholic writer, most likely an Italian religious taking his name from Barberino. Nothing further is asserted here without a source in hand.

Benedict Aretius.affiliation: Professor at the academy of Bern
Benedict Aretius.bio: Benedikt Marti of Bern, who taught Greek and Hebrew and then theology in the Bernese academy. He wrote commentaries across the New Testament and the Examen theologicum, a compact ordering of Protestant doctrine that went through many editions as a student text. He took part in the Bernese proceedings against the antitrinitarian Valentino Gentile, executed in 1566, and published an account of the case that became a source for the history of the antitrinitarian movement. He also collected and described alpine plants, an interest that ran alongside the theology rather than against it.

Benjamin Pickering.bio: An English Puritan minister of the 1640s, associated with Sussex, who is remembered chiefly for a fast sermon preached before the House of Commons during the civil war. Beyond the preaching and the parliamentary connection, little can be said here with confidence.

Bernhard Hübler.bio: A nineteenth-century German Protestant canonist who taught church law at Berlin. He is read in this collection for his study of the reform work of the Council of Constance and the concordats that Martin V concluded with the nations after his election, the moment at which conciliar reform was converted into a set of bilateral agreements with princes. His approach is legal and documentary, concerned with texts and their force rather than with theology.

Caesar Baronius.affiliation: Cardinal; Vatican Librarian; superior of the Roman Oratory
Caesar Baronius.bio: Drawn into Philip Neri's Oratory as a young man and set by Neri to lecture through church history, a task that grew into the Annales Ecclesiastici: twelve folio volumes running from the incarnation to 1198, published between 1588 and 1607 as the Catholic answer to the Magdeburg Centuries. He succeeded Neri as superior of the Oratory, was made cardinal by Clement VIII in 1596 and appointed Vatican Librarian, and revised the Roman Martyrology. The Annales are polemical and archival at once, and later scholars spent two centuries both correcting and continuing them.

Calybute Downing.affiliation: Vicar of Hackney; named to the Westminster Assembly
Calybute Downing.bio: English clergyman whose Discourse of the State Ecclesiasticall (1632) argued for the standing of the church within the commonwealth. In 1640 he preached to the Artillery Company in London that arms might lawfully be taken up in defense of religion, a sermon that forced him into hiding and made him a name in the resistance controversy. He served as a chaplain in the Earl of Essex's parliamentary army and was named to the Westminster Assembly, but died in 1644, before the bulk of its work on the Confession and catechisms was done.

Camillo Mazzella.affiliation: Cardinal; professor at Woodstock College and the Gregorian University
Camillo Mazzella.bio: Italian Jesuit who taught dogmatic theology at Woodstock College in Maryland, shaping the seminary teaching of the American Jesuits, before being called to the Gregorian in Rome. His Latin treatises De Deo creante, De gratia Christi, De virtutibus infusis and De religione et ecclesia are textbooks of the Thomist revival that Leo XIII promoted, written to be dictated and defended in class. Leo made him a cardinal in 1886 and he later held curial office over studies. He is read as a witness to what neo-scholastic theology looked like in its teaching form.

Carlo Passaglia.affiliation: Collegio Romano; later professor at Turin
Carlo Passaglia.bio: Roman Jesuit theologian who taught at the Collegio Romano and worked, with Clemens Schrader, on the theological preparation of the 1854 definition of the Immaculate Conception. His De Ecclesia Christi drew its account of the church as the body of Christ from the fathers rather than the schools, and is read as an anticipation of later patristic ecclesiology. He left the Society, and in the crisis of Italian unification published a plea that the pope surrender the temporal power, for which he was censured. He taught philosophy at Turin and was reconciled to the church before his death.

Caspar Olevian.affiliation: Preacher and church organizer at Heidelberg; later at Herborn
Caspar Olevian.bio: Born at Trier and trained in law in France before turning to the Reformation, he was driven from his native city after preaching there in 1559. At Heidelberg under Frederick III he worked chiefly on church order and discipline, and tradition long paired him with Zacharias Ursinus as a framer of the Heidelberg Catechism of 1563, though his share in the text is now disputed. After 1576 he served the counts of Nassau and helped establish the academy at Herborn. De substantia foederis gratuiti inter Deum et electos is a founding statement of Reformed covenant theology.

Charles Journet.affiliation: Professor of dogmatic theology, seminary of Fribourg; Cardinal from 1965
Charles Journet.bio: Swiss priest who taught dogmatic theology at the Fribourg seminary for four decades. With Jacques Maritain he founded the review Nova et Vetera. His three-volume L'Église du Verbe incarné treats the church through its causes in Thomist fashion and is the most sustained Catholic ecclesiology of the mid-century, written before and carried into the years of the Second Vatican Council, at which he took part. He also wrote on the problem of evil and on grace. Paul VI made him a cardinal in 1965. He is read for ecclesiology done as metaphysics rather than as sociology.

Christian Pesch.affiliation: Jesuit houses of study at Ditton Hall and Valkenburg
Christian Pesch.bio: German Jesuit dogmatic theologian who taught in exile after the Kulturkampf expelled the order from Germany, first in England and then at Valkenburg in the Netherlands. His nine-volume Praelectiones dogmaticae, with the shorter compendium drawn from it, was one of the standard Latin seminary courses of the early twentieth century, ordered around theses, proofs and objections. He is read now less for original argument than as a clear and complete statement of what neo-scholastic dogmatics taught before the return to patristic sources changed the manuals.

Christoph Wittich.affiliation: Professor of theology at Duisburg, Nijmegen and Leiden
Christoph Wittich.bio: Reformed theologian who argued that Scripture speaks of the natural world in the language of ordinary appearance, and so does not settle questions of astronomy: the sun standing still over Gibeon leaves Copernicus untouched. He made the case in Consensus veritatis (1659) and Theologia pacifica (1671), which set him at the center of the Dutch quarrel over Descartes and drew sustained attack from the Voetian party, Andreas Essenius among them. His Anti-Spinoza defended Cartesian philosophy against the charge that it led to Spinoza. A useful figure for how accommodation was argued in the seventeenth century.

Christopher Cartwright.bio: English divine who spent his working life in York and is read for his Hebrew and rabbinic learning rather than for the ecclesiastical politics of the period. His Mellificium Hebraicum gathered rabbinic material bearing on the Old Testament and was printed among the apparatus of the Critici Sacri, and his Electa Thargumico-Rabbinica worked over the Targums. He should not be confused with Thomas Cartwright, the Elizabethan presbyterian; Christopher was of the conforming and royalist side. He belongs in a library of this kind as a specimen of English Christian Hebraism.

Conrad Vorstius.affiliation: Professor at the academy of Steinfurt; appointed to Leiden, 1610
Conrad Vorstius.bio: Born at Cologne and long a teacher at Steinfurt, he was called in 1610 to the Leiden chair left by Arminius. His Tractatus theologicus de Deo, with its account of the divine essence and attributes, drew the charge of Socinianism; James I of England had it burned and pressed the States General against the appointment, and Vorstius never in fact taught at Leiden. The Synod of Dort deposed and banished him in 1619. He died in Holstein three years later. The case is a standing example of how doctrine, patronage and foreign policy ran together.

Cornelius Burges.affiliation: Assessor of the Westminster Assembly; vicar of Watford
Cornelius Burges.bio: Preached before the House of Commons at the opening of the Long Parliament in November 1640, one of the sermons that set the tone for what followed. He served as one of the two assessors of the Westminster Assembly, moderating its business under the prolocutor William Twisse, and was among its most frequent speakers. He promoted the Solemn League and Covenant, but opposed the trial and execution of the king. He bought cathedral lands at Wells during the interregnum and lost them at the Restoration, dying in poverty.

Cornelius Jansen.affiliation: Professor of Scripture at Louvain; Bishop of Ypres from 1636
Cornelius Jansen.bio: Dutch-born theologian who studied at Louvain and Paris, where he formed the friendship with Jean du Vergier de Hauranne, later abbot of Saint-Cyran, that carried his ideas into France. He taught Scripture at Louvain, wrote Mars Gallicus against French alliances with Protestant powers, and was made bishop of Ypres in 1636. His Augustinus, three books on grace, freedom and predestination assembled from Augustine against the Jesuit theology of Molina, appeared after his death and was condemned in the five propositions of Cum occasione in 1653. He is not the earlier Cornelius Jansen, bishop of Ghent.

Costanzo Boccadifuoco.bio: An Italian name; no reliable account of this figure can be given here.

Council of Pisa (acta).bio: The council met at Pisa in 1409, summoned by cardinals who had abandoned both claimants in the Great Western Schism, the Roman Gregory XII and the Avignon Benedict XIII. It declared both deposed as schismatics and elected Peter of Candia as Alexander V. Neither deposed pope submitted, so the practical result was a third line of claimants, and the schism was closed only at Constance between 1414 and 1418. Its standing as an ecumenical council has never been settled. The acta are the surviving record of its sessions and sentences, read chiefly as evidence of conciliarist theory put into practice.

Daniel Cawdrey.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; rector of Great Billing, Northamptonshire
Daniel Cawdrey.bio: Cawdrey sat in the Westminster Assembly and held the rectory of Great Billing in Northamptonshire, losing it at the Restoration settlement. He argued for a strict Sabbath in Sabbatum Redivivum, written with Herbert Palmer, and spent much of the 1650s contesting Congregational polity, chiefly with John Owen, in Independencie a Great Schism and its sequels. He is read now not for original divinity but as a plain statement of the Presbyterian case against the gathered church, made by a man who had sat with the Independents in the Assembly and knew their arguments at first hand.

David Derodon.affiliation: Professor of philosophy at Die, Orange, Nîmes and Geneva
David Derodon.bio: Derodon taught philosophy in the Huguenot academies of the Midi and then at Geneva. He wrote on logic and natural philosophy, pressing hard against received Aristotelian physics, but he is remembered chiefly for Le Tombeau de la Messe, an attack on the sacrifice of the Mass that was condemned by the French authorities and drove him out of the kingdom. Readers come to him for the polemical edge of late Huguenot controversy and for the sight of a working philosopher turning his habits of argument on sacramental theology.

Denis Pétau.affiliation: Professor of rhetoric and then theology, Collège de Clermont, Paris
Denis Pétau.bio: Pétau, who published as Dionysius Petavius, was the leading Jesuit scholar of chronology and patristics of his generation. De doctrina temporum reset technical chronology on new foundations, and the unfinished Dogmata theologica treated Christian doctrine historically, tracing what the fathers actually said rather than arranging conclusions under scholastic heads. His candid account of loose ante-Nicene Trinitarian language was seized on by Arians and Socinians and defended by others as simple honesty. He is the standard instance of humanist erudition turned to dogmatic use.

Dominique Bouix.bio: Bouix produced a long series of Latin treatises on canon law, each covering one institution: the Roman curia, bishops, parish priests, religious, the liturgy, judicial procedure. Written in the decades before the 1917 code, they gather the working law of the Church from decretals, curial decisions and custom, and they argue an ultramontane line on papal jurisdiction throughout. He is consulted as a compact witness to what canon law looked like in practice on the eve of the First Vatican Council.

Durand of Saint-Pourçain.affiliation: Bishop of Limoux, then Le Puy, then Meaux
Durand of Saint-Pourçain.bio: Durand entered the Dominicans and lectured on the Sentences at Paris, revising his commentary through three redactions as his order pressed him toward Thomas Aquinas. He would not be pressed far. He denied that cognition requires intelligible species and cut back the causal machinery in the Thomist account of grace and the sacraments, drawing up lists of censured articles from his own brethren and the name Doctor Resolutissimus with them. He later held three sees in succession and took part in the controversy over the beatific vision under John XXII.

Edmond Richer.affiliation: Syndic of the Faculty of Theology, University of Paris
Edmond Richer.bio: Richer, as syndic of the Paris theology faculty, published in 1611 a short Libellus on ecclesiastical and political power. It argued that Christ gave the keys to the whole Church, that jurisdiction belongs to the body of pastors with the pope as its executive head, and that the temporal order is not subject to Rome. The book cost him the syndicate and was condemned by French bishops, and he was pressed for a retraction in his last years. Richerism named the position thereafter, feeding eighteenth-century Gallicanism and, through it, the constitutional church of the Revolution.

Edmund Staunton.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford; vicar of Kingston upon Thames
Edmund Staunton.bio: Staunton preached at Kingston upon Thames for two decades and sat in the Westminster Assembly. Under the parliamentary visitation of Oxford he was installed as president of Corpus Christi College, holding the place until the Restoration removed him, and he was ejected from ministry in 1662, after which he preached to a private congregation. What survives in print is mostly occasional: funeral sermons and sermons preached before Parliament. He belongs in this library as one of the Assembly's working members rather than as an author with a system to expound.

Edward Corbet.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; fellow of Merton College, Oxford; rector of Haseley, Oxfordshire
Edward Corbet.bio: Corbet was a fellow of Merton College and one of the divines named to the Westminster Assembly. He preached before the House of Commons in the early 1640s and held the rectory of Haseley in Oxfordshire until his death. Little of his work beyond such occasional sermons reached print, and his place here rests on the Assembly seat rather than on a body of writing.

Edward Reynolds.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; Dean of Christ Church and Vice-Chancellor of Oxford; Bishop of Norwich from 1661
Edward Reynolds.bio: Reynolds sat in the Westminster Assembly and served the parliamentary regime at Oxford, then conformed at the Restoration and accepted the see of Norwich, one of very few Presbyterians who did. His Treatise of the Passions and Faculties of the Soule of Man is a long work of moral psychology in the older manner, and he preached and published steadily on Scripture across four decades. Most readers meet him without knowing it, since the General Thanksgiving in the 1662 Book of Common Prayer is his composition.

Edward Stillingfleet.tradition: Church of England; latitudinarian in temper, conformist in discipline
Edward Stillingfleet.affiliation: Dean of St Paul's; Bishop of Worcester from 1689
Edward Stillingfleet.bio: Stillingfleet made his name young with Irenicum, which argued that no one form of church government is fixed by divine law, and with Origines Sacrae, a defence of revealed religion mounted on historical and philological ground. He then wrote at length against Rome, and against nonconformity in The Mischief of Separation, having in effect abandoned the irenic case of his youth. Late in life he pressed John Locke on whether the new way of ideas left room for the doctrine of the Trinity, an exchange philosophers still read.

Emmanuel Schelstrate.bio: Schelstrate, a Fleming trained at Antwerp, was brought to Rome and put in charge of the Vatican Library. He worked on the early African church and on the acts of the Council of Constance, disputing the Gallican reading of the decree Haec sancta, and he wrote on the discipline of the secret, the early church's practice of withholding its mysteries from the uninitiated. His scholarship is inseparable from the papal and conciliar quarrel of the 1680s, in which he supplied Rome with its documentary case against the Gallican Articles of 1682.

Festus Hommius.affiliation: Secretary of the Synod of Dort; regent of the Statencollege, Leiden
Festus Hommius.bio: Hommius was a Leiden minister who led the contra-Remonstrant side in the years before Dort and served as one of the synod's secretaries, so the record of those sessions passed through his hands. He put the Belgic Confession into Latin for the foreign delegates and drew up the Specimen controversiarum Belgicarum, a point by point statement of what the Remonstrants were held to teach. He afterwards ran the Statencollege at Leiden and had a hand in the States translation of the Bible.

Francis Cheynell.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; President of St John's College, Oxford
Francis Cheynell.bio: Cheynell sat in the Westminster Assembly and was installed by the parliamentary visitors as president of St John's College, Oxford, losing the place at the Restoration. He wrote against Socinianism at length, in The Rise, Growth and Danger of Socinianisme and The Divine Triunity, treating anti-Trinitarianism as a rising danger rather than a spent one. He is remembered as much for temper as for doctrine, since his attendance on the dying William Chillingworth, and his burial of Chillingworth's book with him, became the standing anecdote against Puritan zeal.

Francis Taylor.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; rector of Yalding, Kent, and later at Canterbury
Francis Taylor.bio: Taylor served parishes in Kent and was named to the Westminster Assembly. His printed work is that of a Hebraist and expositor: a commentary on Proverbs and a Latin edition, with notes, of the rabbinic tractate Pirke Aboth, which put a Jewish source into English Protestant hands. Beyond the Assembly seat and this small body of exegetical work, little of his life is recorded.

Francis Woodcock.bio: Woodcock was one of the members of the Westminster Assembly and preached before Parliament on the appointed fast days in the 1640s. Those sermons are most of what survives from him in print, and he died young. His place here is the Assembly seat and that handful of occasional sermons.

Francisco de Oviedo.bio: A Spanish Jesuit of the seventeenth century, author of a philosophical course of the kind produced for teaching in Jesuit colleges. Nothing further is asserted here.

Franciscus Sylvius.affiliation: Professor and dean of the faculty of theology, University of Douai
Franciscus Sylvius.bio: Sylvius, born François Du Bois, spent his career at Douai, where he taught theology and served as dean of the faculty. His commentaries on the Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas were reprinted for two centuries and were among the ordinary working tools of seminary teaching; he also wrote catechetical and devotional pieces. He is a fair specimen of Counter-Reformation Thomism as it was actually taught, close to the text of Aquinas and wary of speculative excursions.

Frans Burman.affiliation: Professor of theology, University of Utrecht
Frans Burman.bio: Burman taught at Utrecht and wrote the Synopsis theologiae, a full system built on the succession of divine covenants in the manner of Johannes Cocceius. He was also a Cartesian, and the pairing set him firmly on one side of the long Dutch quarrel between Voetians and Cocceians over philosophy, biblical interpretation and the Sabbath. Historians of philosophy know him for another reason: as a student he interviewed Descartes in 1648, and the notes of that conversation are among the few records of Descartes explaining himself in speech.

Franz Vidmar.bio: Nothing can be said of this figure with confidence beyond the name, which is central European in form.

Gaspar Hickes.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; vicar of Landrake, Cornwall
Gaspar Hickes.bio: Hickes held the Cornish living of Landrake and was named to the Westminster Assembly, among the few members drawn from the far west. He preached before Parliament on the appointed fast days, and those sermons are the bulk of his printed output. He was ejected in 1662 under the Act of Uniformity. Like much of the Assembly's rank and file, he is known by the seat he held rather than by a body of divinity.

Gellius Snecanus.bio: Snecanus, a Frisian minister whose name marks him as from Sneek, wrote on predestination in terms that resisted the harder Reformed statements of his day. His reading of Romans 9 took the chapter to concern God's dealings with peoples rather than the eternal fate of individuals, and writers in the later Arminian controversy cited him as a Dutch precedent for their own case. He is worth meeting as evidence that the dispute settled at Dort had older roots inside the Dutch Reformed ministry itself.

Gennadius Scholarios, Patriarch of Const.affiliation: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, in three terms from 1454
Gennadius Scholarios, Patriarch of Const.bio: George Scholarios was a lay judge and philosopher at the Byzantine court who attended the Council of Ferrara and Florence and at first spoke for union with Rome. He changed his mind, took the monastic name Gennadios, and after the death of Mark of Ephesus led the party that refused the union. When Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453 he was made patriarch of the surviving Christian population, and he wrote a short account of the faith for the sultan. He translated and used Thomas Aquinas while rejecting Latin doctrine, which makes him hard to place and worth reading.

Georg Dedeken.bio: Dedeken, a Hamburg pastor, compiled the Thesaurus consiliorum et decisionum, a large collection of written opinions issued by Lutheran theological faculties and individual theologians on questions of doctrine, church order, marriage and conscience. The value of such a book is that it shows Lutheran orthodoxy answering practical cases rather than composing systems, and it stayed in use as a working reference for pastors and consistories long after his death.

Georg Müller.bio: The name is common in German Lutheran and Reformed sources and belongs to several distinct figures; without further identifying detail no account is given here.

George Cassander.affiliation: Flemish lay theologian; consulted by the imperial court
George Cassander.bio: Cassander spent his life looking for terms on which Catholics and Protestants could remain one church. De officio pii viri urged Christians to stay within the old communion while working for its reform, and the Consultatio went through the disputed articles of the Augsburg Confession seeking a reading both sides could accept, using the consensus of the ancient church as the measure. Neither side thanked him. His works were placed on the Index and Calvin answered him sharply. He is the standard case of sixteenth-century irenicism, and of its failure.

George Gillespie.affiliation: Scottish commissioner to the Westminster Assembly; minister at Wemyss, then Edinburgh; Moderator of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, 1648
George Gillespie.bio: Gillespie published A Dispute against the English Popish Ceremonies at twenty-four, against the imposition of kneeling, holy days and the rest of the Perth Articles on the Scottish church. He was one of the Scottish commissioners sent to the Westminster Assembly and spoke there often. Aaron's Rod Blossoming is the fullest Presbyterian argument produced in that debate against Erastian control of church discipline, distinguishing the two kingdoms without surrendering either to the other. He died at thirty-five, months after being chosen moderator of the Church of Scotland's General Assembly.

George Walker.affiliation: Rector of St John the Evangelist, Watling Street, London; member of the Westminster Assembly
George Walker.bio: Walker held a London city living for some four decades and was named to the Westminster Assembly. Most of his printed work is controversy: a long quarrel with Anthony Wotton over whether Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer, a second front against John Goodwin on justification, and a running polemic against Roman Catholic apologists. He also wrote The Doctrine of the Sabbath, arguing the strict Sabbatarian position most of his Assembly colleagues held. He repays reading as a specimen of the London Puritan controversialist rather than as a systematic divine.

Gerardus Joannes Vossius.affiliation: Regent of the States College and professor at Leiden; first professor of history at the Athenaeum Illustre, Amsterdam
Gerardus Joannes Vossius.bio: Vossius was a philologist and historian who did theology the way a humanist does it, by tracing the sources. His history of the Pelagian controversy, published in 1618, reconstructed that quarrel so evenhandedly that it cost him his Leiden post in the aftermath of Dort, since the Contra-Remonstrants read the fairness as advocacy. He also produced De historicis Graecis and De historicis Latinis, a large body of grammatical and rhetorical work, and De theologia gentili, an early comparative treatment of pagan religion. He moved to Amsterdam in 1632 to teach history at the new Athenaeum.

Gilbert Jack.tradition: Reformed background; Scot teaching in the Dutch Republic
Gilbert Jack.affiliation: Professor of philosophy at the University of Leiden
Gilbert Jack.bio: Jack, or Jacchaeus, was an Aberdeen Scot who spent his working life at Leiden, where he taught philosophy for roughly a quarter century and also lectured in medicine. His Institutiones physicae and Primae philosophiae institutiones were textbooks of a moderate, Christianized Aristotelianism, reprinted often enough to shape how a generation of Dutch and Scottish students first met natural philosophy. The stricter Reformed party in the Netherlands thought his confessional position suspect and accused him of leaning toward Rome and toward Arminius. He kept his chair until his death.

Giovanni Domenico Mansi.affiliation: Clerk Regular of the Mother of God, Lucca; Archbishop of Lucca from 1765
Giovanni Domenico Mansi.bio: Mansi is the reason most readers can get at conciliar acta at all. His Sacrorum Conciliorum Nova et Amplissima Collectio, begun in 1759, gathered the decrees and surrounding documents of the councils from the early synods forward, building on the earlier Labbe and Coleti collections and correcting them. It reached thirty-one folio volumes covering the councils down to the fifteenth century; later editors continued and reprinted the work, and the modern set runs to fifty-three volumes. A citation to a council by volume and column number is still normally a citation to Mansi. He also edited Baronius and wrote on liturgy.

Giovanni Perrone.affiliation: Professor of dogmatic theology and rector of the Roman College
Giovanni Perrone.bio: Perrone taught dogmatics at the Roman College for most of the nineteenth century, and his Praelectiones theologicae became the seminary manual against which neo-scholastic theology measured itself, abridged and translated across Europe and America. His De Immaculato B. V. Mariae Conceptu of 1847 argued that the doctrine was definable and fed directly into the definition of 1854. When Newman was in Rome he submitted his theory of doctrinal development to Perrone; the resulting objections and replies survive and remain the sharpest early Roman engagement with the Essay on Development.

Girolamo Zanchi.affiliation: Professor of Old Testament at Strasbourg; pastor at Chiavenna; professor of theology at Heidelberg and at the Casimirianum, Neustadt
Girolamo Zanchi.bio: Zanchi entered the Augustinian canons at Bergamo, where Peter Martyr Vermigli's lectures turned him toward the Reformation. He left Italy in 1551 and never returned. At Strasbourg he taught the Old Testament and quarrelled with Johann Marbach over predestination and perseverance, a dispute that drove him first to Chiavenna and then to the Palatinate. De tribus Elohim defended Nicene trinitarianism against antitrinitarians, De natura Dei is a full scholastic doctrine of God, and De religione christiana fides is his mature confession. He is the standard example of Aristotelian method put to Reformed dogmatic use.

Glassius, Salomon.affiliation: Professor at Jena; General Superintendent of Gotha under Duke Ernest the Pious
Glassius, Salomon.bio: Glassius studied under Johann Gerhard at Jena and later served Duke Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha as General Superintendent, with a hand in the duchy's church ordinances and its school reform. Philologia sacra, first published in 1623, is the work he is read for: a systematic account of the grammar, idiom and figurative speech of the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures, written to keep exegesis tied to the text rather than to dogmatic convenience. It stayed in use for a century and a half and marks the high point of Lutheran orthodox hermeneutics before the historical-critical turn.

Heinrich Bullinger.bio: Bullinger took charge of the Zurich church weeks after Zwingli was killed at Kappel and held it for forty-four years, which made him the steadiest of the first-generation Reformed leaders. The Decades, fifty sermons covering the whole of Christian doctrine, were prescribed reading for English clergy under Elizabeth. He negotiated the Consensus Tigurinus with Calvin in 1549, settling the eucharistic difference between Zurich and Geneva. The Second Helvetic Confession of 1566 is his; it became the most widely adopted Reformed confession on the continent. His surviving correspondence runs to roughly twelve thousand letters.

Heinrich Finke (ed.).tradition: Roman Catholic; German academic church history
Heinrich Finke (ed.).affiliation: Professor of history at Freiburg im Breisgau
Heinrich Finke (ed.).bio: Finke was a German Catholic historian of the later Middle Ages whose lasting service was documentary. His Acta Concilii Constanciensis, issued in four volumes from 1896 onward, assembled the letters, protocols, diaries and diplomatic papers surrounding the Council of Constance and put study of the council on a footing that earlier printed collections could not provide. A reader meeting his name in this library is meeting an editor rather than an author: what is his is the apparatus, the dating, and the judgment about what belonged in the record.

Heinrich Höpfner.bio: A German Lutheran theologian of the seventeenth century, associated with the theological faculty at Leipzig during the period of confessional orthodoxy.

Henry Hall.bio: An English minister who appears among the divines summoned to the Westminster Assembly. Little beyond that membership can be stated about him with confidence.

Henry Hammond.tradition: Church of England; Laudian and royalist
Henry Hammond.affiliation: Rector of Penshurst, Kent; Archdeacon of Chichester; canon of Christ Church, Oxford; chaplain to Charles I
Henry Hammond.bio: Hammond was the leading Anglican theologian of the Interregnum, and largely the man who kept episcopalian divinity in print while it had no church left to be preached in. A Practical Catechism of 1644 set out a moral theology in which obedience is integral to saving faith, a position his Calvinist critics read as Arminian. His Paraphrase and Annotations upon the New Testament of 1653 was the first substantial English critical commentary of its kind. Of Schisme answered the Roman charge that the English church had separated itself. He supported ejected clergy out of his own pocket and died shortly before the Restoration.

Henry Roborough.affiliation: Scribe of the Westminster Assembly; minister of St Leonard, Eastcheap, London
Henry Roborough.bio: Roborough was one of the two scribes of the Westminster Assembly, sharing the duty with Adoniram Byfield. The office matters more than the title suggests, since the sessions were closed and the divines sworn to secrecy, and nearly everything known about the Assembly's debates comes from the minutes the scribes kept. He held a London city living at St Leonard, Eastcheap. He published almost nothing, and his place in the record is the record itself.

Henry Tozer.bio: Tozer was a fellow of Exeter College, Oxford, a preacher of Calvinist conviction who was nonetheless removed from the university by the parliamentary visitors and spent his last years abroad.

Henry Wilkinson, Jr..affiliation: Principal of Magdalen Hall, Oxford; member of the Westminster Assembly
Henry Wilkinson, Jr..bio: The Westminster rolls distinguish two Henry Wilkinsons, father and son, and this is the younger; Oxford men called him Long Harry to keep him apart from the other Henry Wilkinson at Christ Church. He sat in the Assembly, held the Principalship of Magdalen Hall through the Interregnum, and was one of the university's appointed preachers. The Act of Uniformity put him out in 1662, after which he preached to a gathered congregation. What survives of his writing is sermons; the Assembly membership and the Oxford office are why the name is here.

Herbert Palmer.affiliation: Master of Queens' College, Cambridge; assessor of the Westminster Assembly; rector of Ashwell, Hertfordshire
Herbert Palmer.bio: Palmer was a catechist by temperament. His Endeavour of Making the Principles of Christian Religion Plaine and Easie put the faith into short question and answer for children and went through many editions, and he was among the divines pressing the Assembly toward a form brief enough to be memorized. Parliament made him Master of Queens' College, Cambridge, and the Assembly chose him as one of its assessors. Preaching before Parliament in 1644 he attacked toleration and took public notice of Milton's divorce tract. Memorials of Godliness and Christianity collects his devotional work. He died before the Assembly finished its business.

Herman Witsius.affiliation: Professor of theology at Franeker, Utrecht and Leiden
Herman Witsius.bio: Witsius wrote covenant theology in the middle of a Dutch quarrel about it. De oeconomia foederum Dei cum hominibus, published in 1677, laid out the covenants of works and grace with enough care to be read by Voetians and Cocceians alike. Translated in the eighteenth century, it became the standard English introduction to federal theology. His Exercitationes sacrae on the Apostles' Creed and on the Lord's Prayer are patient expositions rather than polemics. Pastors go to him for the structure of redemptive history set out without partisanship, and for a temper unusual among seventeenth-century Dutch controversialists.

Hermann von der Hardt.affiliation: Professor of oriental languages at Helmstedt
Hermann von der Hardt.bio: Von der Hardt taught Hebrew and oriental languages at Helmstedt and in his early career moved in the Pietist circles around Spener. His Magnum Oecumenicum Constantiense Concilium, six folio volumes issued from 1697, printed the diaries, treatises and acts of the Council of Constance and remained the fullest documentary basis for study of that council until modern editions appeared. His later exegetical work, which read Jonah, Esther and other books as allegories of ancient history, was rejected in his own lifetime and left his reputation divided: an indispensable editor and an eccentric interpreter.

Hubert Jedin (ed.).affiliation: Professor of church history at Bonn; consultant at the Second Vatican Council
Hubert Jedin (ed.).bio: Jedin wrote the history of Trent that displaced every earlier account, Catholic and Protestant alike. Geschichte des Konzils von Trient, four volumes over three decades, worked from the council's own archives and treated it as a contested political and theological event rather than a monolith. His distinction between Catholic Reform and Counter-Reformation reset the vocabulary of the field. He also directed the Handbuch der Kirchengeschichte, the multivolume cooperative church history that carries his name as editor, and served as a consultant at Vatican II, where the precedent of Trent was constantly in play.

Humphrey Chambers.bio: Chambers was a West Country minister, holding livings in Somerset and then Wiltshire, who was named to the Westminster Assembly and took part in its work. Under the Protectorate he served among the commissioners charged with examining candidates for the ministry. He lost his living at the Restoration. He published very little, and his public significance is the Assembly membership rather than a body of writing.

Isaac Barrow.affiliation: First Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, Cambridge; Regius Professor of Greek; Master of Trinity College, Cambridge
Isaac Barrow.bio: Barrow held the Lucasian chair in mathematics and resigned it in 1669 in favour of his student Newton, then turned to divinity and later to the mastership of Trinity. His geometrical lectures worked tangent and area problems close to the calculus Newton would formalize. As a divine he is read for the sermons, admired for a long, exact, unhurried prose that later writers treated as a model, and for A Treatise of the Pope's Supremacy, the most thorough English argument against papal jurisdiction produced in the seventeenth century. His expositions of the Creed, Decalogue and sacraments appeared after his death.

Jacobus Trigland.affiliation: Minister at Amsterdam; professor of theology at Leiden
Jacobus Trigland.bio: Trigland preached at Amsterdam through the years of the Arminian crisis and was one of the harder Contra-Remonstrant voices in the city, taking a theological chair at Leiden later in life. His Kerckelycke Geschiedenissen of 1650 is a history of the Dutch church written explicitly against the Remonstrant account Uytenbogaert had published, and the two books are best read together as rival memories of the same events. The rest of his output is polemical and antiquarian, defending the settlement reached at Dort.

Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples.affiliation: Paris; the Meaux circle under Bishop Guillaume Briçonnet; the court of Marguerite de Navarre at Nérac
Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples.bio: Lefèvre began as an editor of Aristotle and moved to Scripture. The Quincuplex Psalterium of 1509 printed five Latin psalters in parallel, and his commentary on the Pauline epistles of 1512 argued for justification by faith and against merit several years before Luther, though from inside the Roman church. At Meaux he joined Briçonnet's attempt at diocesan reform through preaching and vernacular Bible reading. The Sorbonne condemned him and he fled more than once. He translated the New Testament into French in 1523 and the whole Bible by 1530, and he died under Marguerite de Navarre's protection without ever leaving the old church.

Jacques Lenfant.affiliation: Minister to the French Reformed congregation at Berlin; chaplain to the Prussian court
Jacques Lenfant.bio: Lenfant was a Huguenot refugee who spent his career preaching to the French church in Berlin and writing the history of the fifteenth-century councils from a Protestant vantage. His Histoire du Concile de Constance of 1714 and Histoire du Concile de Pise of 1724, with a companion history of the Hussite wars and the Council of Basel, treated conciliarism and the burning of Hus as the church's own repudiated attempt at reform. The books were read across Europe, answered at length by Catholic historians, and did much to fix the Protestant memory of Constance.

James Durham.affiliation: Minister at Glasgow; chaplain to Charles II
James Durham.bio: Durham died at thirty-six and left work that Scottish and English readers kept reprinting for two centuries. The Dying Man's Testament to the Church of Scotland, better known as his treatise on scandal, is the most careful Reformed handling of division, offence and the limits of separation written in the aftermath of the Protester and Resolutioner split. He composed it while dying. Clavis Cantici expounds the Song of Songs, and his commentary on Revelation and his exposition of the Ten Commandments were long standard. Pastors still go to him on unity and on when a church may be left.

Jean Gerson.affiliation: Chancellor of the University of Paris from 1395
Jean Gerson.bio: Gerson was the most audible voice at Constance and the one who pressed hardest for the council's authority to end the schism by deposing rival claimants, an argument set out in De potestate ecclesiastica and De unitate ecclesiae. He also fought and lost the attempt to have Jean Petit's defence of tyrannicide condemned, which kept him from returning safely to France; he ended his life at Lyon. Alongside the ecclesiology he wrote a large body of pastoral and mystical theology, including De mystica theologia and treatises on the discernment of spirits, and sermons in French for ordinary hearers.

Jeremiah Burroughs.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; preacher at Stepney and Cripplegate, London
Jeremiah Burroughs.bio: Burroughs was one of the five Dissenting Brethren who put out An Apologeticall Narration in 1643, asking the Assembly and Parliament for room for congregational churches inside a national settlement. He made the case without rancour, and his Irenicum, to the Lovers of Truth and Peace is a plea against the hardening of parties on both sides. He is now read mostly for the practical divinity: The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment, Gospel Worship, and the long exposition of Hosea. He spent the 1630s in exile in Rotterdam and drew large London congregations after his return.

Jeremy Taylor.affiliation: Chaplain to Archbishop Laud and to Charles I; Bishop of Down and Connor; Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College Dublin
Jeremy Taylor.bio: Taylor wrote Holy Living in 1650 and Holy Dying in 1651 while sheltering in Wales after the royalist defeat. The two books carried Anglican piety through the Interregnum and long past it. The Liberty of Prophesying argued for restraint in imposing articles beyond the Creed, a position he showed markedly less enthusiasm for once he held a bishopric in Ulster among Presbyterians. Ductor Dubitantium is his enormous work of casuistry. Unum Necessarium, which handled original sin in terms his fellow bishops thought Pelagian, cost him support. He is read for the prose quite as much as for the doctrine.

Joannes Poncius.bio: Irish Franciscan, known in his own country as John Punch, who taught philosophy and theology at St Isidore's College in Rome, the Irish friary founded by Luke Wadding. He worked with Wadding on the collected edition of the works of Duns Scotus published at Lyons in 1639, and wrote his own Integer philosophiae cursus ad mentem Scoti together with commentaries on Scotus. He is remembered outside Scotist circles for the formula that entities are not to be multiplied beyond necessity, the sentence later attached to William of Ockham.

Johann Baptist Franzelin.affiliation: Professor of Dogmatic Theology, Pontifical Gregorian University; Cardinal
Johann Baptist Franzelin.bio: Tyrolean Jesuit who taught dogmatic theology at the Gregorian University in Rome for two decades and served as a papal theologian at the First Vatican Council, where he had a hand in the schemata that stand behind the constitution Dei Filius. He was created cardinal in 1876. His Tractatus de divina traditione et scriptura is the work he is read for: an account of tradition as a living transmission carried by the teaching church rather than a second deposit of propositions alongside Scripture. He also wrote treatises on the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the sacraments.

Johann Franz Budde.affiliation: Professor of Theology, University of Jena
Johann Franz Budde.bio: German Lutheran who taught moral philosophy at Halle before moving to the theological faculty at Jena, where he spent the rest of his career. Latinized as Buddeus. His Institutiones theologiae dogmaticae and Institutiones theologiae moralis were widely used textbooks, and he wrote extensively in church history and in the history of philosophy. He stands at the seam where Lutheran scholastic orthodoxy meets Pietism and the early Enlightenment: sympathetic to Spener's concern for practical godliness, and a public opponent of Christian Wolff, whose rationalist system he judged corrosive of revealed doctrine.

Johann Ludwig Fabricius.affiliation: Professor of Theology, University of Heidelberg
Johann Ludwig Fabricius.bio: Reformed theologian at Heidelberg, where he held a chair in the theological faculty, served repeatedly as rector, and acted as church councillor to the Elector Palatine Karl Ludwig. His temper was irenic, in keeping with the confessionally mixed Palatinate of his day. He is best remembered outside specialist literature for a letter he did not want to write: in 1673, at the Elector's instruction, he offered Spinoza a chair of philosophy at Heidelberg on condition that he not disturb the established religion, an offer Spinoza declined.

Johann Scharp.bio: The name is Latinized in more than one Protestant tradition in this period, and the figure intended cannot be identified with confidence from the name alone.

Johannes Althusius.affiliation: Syndic of the city of Emden; formerly professor of law, Herborn Academy
Johannes Althusius.bio: German Calvinist jurist who studied at Basel and Geneva, taught law at the Reformed academy in Herborn, and from 1604 served as syndic of the East Frisian city of Emden. His Politica Methodice Digesta, first published in 1603 and enlarged twice, builds the commonwealth upward from the consociation: household, guild, city, province, realm, each with its own right, and sovereignty resting in the associated body rather than in the prince. He also wrote the Dicaeologicae libri tres on jurisprudence. He is read now as a source for federal and covenantal political theory.

Johannes Braun.affiliation: Professor of Theology and Hebrew, University of Groningen
Johannes Braun.bio: Reformed theologian, born in the Palatinate, who served the Walloon congregation at Nijmegen before taking a chair of theology and Hebrew at Groningen. He belonged to the Cocceian and broadly Cartesian party in the Dutch church, and was attacked accordingly by the Voetian side. His Doctrina foederum, sive systema theologiae didacticae et elencticae presents dogmatics on the covenant scheme; he also wrote a commentary on Hebrews and Vestitus sacerdotum Hebraeorum, a detailed study of the priestly garments that was consulted long after his other work was set aside.

Johannes Brenz.affiliation: Provost of the Stiftskirche, Stuttgart; reformer of Württemberg
Johannes Brenz.bio: The reformer of Württemberg. Preacher at Schwäbisch Hall from 1522, where he carried the town over to the reform, and after the Interim provost of the collegiate church in Stuttgart and the architect of the Württemberg church order. His catechism of 1527 was among the earliest and most widely reprinted Lutheran catechisms, and he drafted the Confessio Virtembergica presented to the Council of Trent in 1552. In the eucharistic controversy he defended the ubiquity of Christ's human nature against Reformed objections, a line the Formula of Concord later took up in modified form.

Johannes Cocceius.affiliation: Professor of Theology, University of Leiden; formerly Franeker
Johannes Cocceius.bio: Born at Bremen, taught Hebrew and then theology at Franeker, and from 1650 held the chair of theology at Leiden. His Summa doctrinae de foedere et testamento Dei set covenant and testament at the centre of dogmatics and traced a series of abrogations of the covenant of works through the history of salvation. He was a first-rate Hebraist, author of a lexicon of Hebrew and Aramaic and of commentaries on most of the Bible, and his typological reading of prophecy and history divided the Dutch church against the followers of Gisbertus Voetius for two generations.

Johannes Combach.bio: A German Protestant academic philosopher of the early seventeenth century, associated with Marburg, who published textbook treatments of metaphysics and physics in the scholastic manner then standard in Protestant faculties. Nothing further can be stated here with confidence.

Johannes Greydanus.bio: A Dutch name; the figure is not securely identified, and nothing beyond that can be said responsibly here.

Johannes Oecolampadius.bio: Born Johann Hussgen at Weinsberg and known by the Greek form of his name. A Greek and Hebrew scholar who assisted Erasmus with the Greek New Testament of 1516, he became lecturer and then preacher at Basel and led the city into the reform in 1529. He edited and translated Greek patristic texts, chiefly Chrysostom and John of Damascus, and lectured on Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the minor prophets. At the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 he argued the Swiss case on the Supper alongside Zwingli against Luther, and he died weeks after Zwingli fell at Kappel.

Johannes Vincke (ed.).bio: A German church historian whose scholarly work centred on the medieval church in the Crown of Aragon and its dealings with the papacy, including the years of the Great Western Schism. He appears in this library as an editor rather than an author: the volumes under his name print archival material from Spanish and Vatican collections, so the words in them belong to the medieval documents and the apparatus is his.

Johannes à Marck.affiliation: Professor of Theology, University of Leiden; formerly Franeker and Groningen
Johannes à Marck.bio: Dutch Reformed theologian who held chairs at Franeker and Groningen before settling at Leiden for four decades. His Compendium theologiae christianae didactico-elencticum became the standard classroom dogmatics in the Dutch and, in translation and abridgement, the Scottish Reformed schools well into the eighteenth century, with an expanded version issued as the Christianae theologiae medulla. He also produced commentaries on the minor prophets, on the Song of Songs, and on Revelation, and volumes of exegetical exercitationes. He is read as a late, careful representative of Reformed scholastic method rather than as an innovator.

John Arrowsmith.affiliation: Regius Professor of Divinity, Cambridge; Master of Trinity College
John Arrowsmith.bio: Member of the Westminster Assembly and one of its more frequent speakers. At Cambridge he was Master of St John's College and afterwards of Trinity, and held the Regius chair of divinity. Two books carry his name: Tactica Sacra, which sets out the Christian's conflict under military figures, and Armilla Catechetica, a chain of aphorisms with expanded commentary on the being of God, the authority of Scripture, and creation. Both were published at or near the end of his life and show the Assembly's doctrinal habits worked out in a university register.

John Bond.bio: An English minister who sat in the Westminster Assembly and preached before the Long Parliament during the 1640s, and who held academic office at Cambridge under the Commonwealth. His surviving publications are occasional sermons rather than a body of divinity, and his standing rests on the Assembly membership itself.

John Calvin.affiliation: Pastor of the Church of Geneva
John Calvin.bio: Born at Noyon in Picardy and trained in law at Orléans and Bourges. The Institutio Christianae Religionis appeared at Basel in 1536 as a short defence of persecuted French evangelicals and was rewritten and enlarged until the definitive Latin edition of 1559. He served the church at Geneva from 1536, was expelled in 1538, ministered to the French congregation at Strasbourg, and returned in 1541 to spend the rest of his life there. He left commentaries on nearly the whole Bible, several thousand sermons, the Ecclesiastical Ordinances, the catechism of 1542, and controversial works against Sadoleto, Pighius, Servetus, and Westphal.

John Carter.bio: Several English clergymen of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries bore this name, and the figure intended cannot be securely identified from the name alone.

John Conant.tradition: Reformed; conforming Church of England after 1670
John Conant.affiliation: Regius Professor of Divinity, Oxford; Rector of Exeter College; later Archdeacon of Norwich
John Conant.bio: Rector of Exeter College, Oxford, Regius Professor of Divinity, and Vice-Chancellor of the university during the Interregnum. He took the Presbyterian side at the Savoy Conference of 1661 and lost his places in 1662 for refusing the Act of Uniformity, but conformed in 1670 and ended his life as Archdeacon of Norwich and a prebendary of Worcester. He published little himself; six volumes of his sermons were printed after his death and are the main body of his work. His career is a useful case of the moderate Presbyterian who eventually stayed in.

John Dury.bio: Scots-born minister who gave roughly fifty years to the attempt to reconcile the Lutheran and Reformed churches, travelling between England, the Low Countries, the German states, Scandinavia, and Switzerland to gather subscriptions to an irenic formula that never held. He sat in the Westminster Assembly, worked with Samuel Hartlib and Comenius on schemes for the reform of learning and the advancement of trade and education, and held a post in the royal library under the Commonwealth. His writings are largely occasional pieces and memoranda in the service of that one project.

John Flavel.bio: Presbyterian minister at Dartmouth in Devon, ejected under the Act of Uniformity in 1662, who went on preaching in private houses and in the fields around the town through the years of persecution. He wrote for a congregation of merchants and seafaring people, and the titles show it: Navigation Spiritualized and Husbandry Spiritualized draw doctrine out of ordinary trades. His durable works are The Mystery of Providence, The Fountain of Life, a long series on the offices of Christ, and A Saint Indeed, on keeping the heart. He is read for pastoral application rather than system.

John Greene.bio: An English clergyman of the seventeenth century; the figure cannot be securely identified from the name alone, and nothing further is asserted here.

John Howe.affiliation: Domestic chaplain to Oliver and Richard Cromwell; minister at Silver Street, London
John Howe.bio: Minister at Great Torrington in Devon before he was taken to Whitehall as domestic chaplain to Oliver Cromwell and then to his son Richard. Ejected in 1662, he spent years in Ireland as a chaplain and returned to pastor a London congregation. The Living Temple, his largest work, argues the soul as God's dwelling place against the irreligion he saw around him; The Blessedness of the Righteous and Delighting in God are the practical books he is read for. He worked steadily for accommodation between Presbyterians and Independents and wrote in a deliberately unpolemical register.

John Jackson.bio: More than one English divine of this name is on record, and the figure intended cannot be identified with confidence from the name alone.

John Jewel.bio: Fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, Marian exile at Frankfurt, Strasbourg, and Zurich, where he attached himself to Peter Martyr Vermigli, and from 1560 Bishop of Salisbury. His Challenge Sermon at Paul's Cross in 1559 dared Rome to produce patristic warrant for its disputed practices from the first six hundred years, and set the terms of English controversy for a generation. The Apologia Ecclesiae Anglicanae of 1562 became the semi-official defence of the Elizabethan settlement and was englished by Anne Bacon. The long exchange with Thomas Harding produced his Defence of the Apology.

John Ley.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; sub-dean of Chester
John Ley.bio: Cheshire minister, sub-dean of Chester, and a member of the Westminster Assembly who also served as president of Sion College in London. He was among the divines who produced the Annotations upon All the Books of the Old and New Testament, the commentary commonly called the Westminster Annotations, which was the Assembly circle's chief exegetical monument. His other publications are sermons and occasional controversial pieces on ceremonies and on the Sabbath. Like many of his colleagues, his standing rests on committee work rather than on a system of his own.

John Lightfoot.affiliation: Master of St Catharine's Hall, Cambridge; member of the Westminster Assembly
John Lightfoot.bio: Hebraist and rabbinic scholar, Master of St Catharine's Hall at Cambridge and for a time Vice-Chancellor of the university. He sat in the Westminster Assembly and kept the journal that remains one of the two principal records of its debates, and it preserves his own dissent on several points. His Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae read the Gospels and Acts against Talmudic and midrashic material, making him one of the first Christian scholars to work systematically from rabbinic sources. He also wrote on the temple, the service of the sanctuary, and biblical chronology.

John Maynard.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; rector in Sussex
John Maynard.bio: An English minister who sat in the Westminster Assembly and served a Sussex parish. What survives under his name is a small body of printed sermons, including fast sermons preached before Parliament, rather than a work of divinity; his place in this library rests on the Assembly membership.

John Owen.affiliation: Dean of Christ Church, Oxford; Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford
John Owen.bio: Owen was the leading theologian of English Independency and the most systematic of the Puritans. Cromwell made him Dean of Christ Church in 1651 and Vice-Chancellor of Oxford in 1652, posts the Restoration took from him. He wrote The Death of Death in the Death of Christ (1647) for particular redemption, Of the Mortification of Sin (1656), Communion with God (1657), the Pneumatologia on the Holy Spirit (1674), and a commentary on Hebrews that ran to seven volumes. Readers come to him for Trinitarian doctrine worked out pastorally, and for the fullest defence of congregational polity written from inside the Reformed tradition.

John Pearson.affiliation: Lady Margaret Professor of Divinity, Cambridge; Master of Trinity College; Bishop of Chester
John Pearson.bio: Pearson was a scholar of the Laudian formation who rose after the Restoration to the Lady Margaret professorship at Cambridge, the mastership of Trinity College, and the see of Chester. An Exposition of the Creed (1659), grown out of sermons preached at St Clement's, Eastcheap, became the standard English commentary on the Apostles' Creed and stayed in ordination reading lists for two centuries. His Vindiciae Epistolarum S. Ignatii (1672) defended the authenticity of the Ignatian letters against Daillé and settled the question for a generation. Read him for patristic argument conducted in plain English.

John Preston.affiliation: Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge; preacher at Lincoln's Inn
John Preston.bio: Preston turned academic preferment into a pulpit. He became Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 1622, held the Trinity Church lectureship there, preached at Lincoln's Inn, and served for a time as chaplain to Prince Charles under the patronage of the Duke of Buckingham. Almost everything under his name appeared after his early death, edited by Richard Sibbes and John Davenport: The New Covenant, The Breastplate of Faith and Love, Life Eternall. He is read for the covenant theology and the preaching of assurance that shaped a generation of ministers in England and New England.

John Selden.affiliation: Member of Parliament; lay member of the Westminster Assembly
John Selden.bio: Selden was a common lawyer, orientalist and parliamentarian, and one of the laymen the Long Parliament sent to sit with the Westminster Assembly, where his command of rabbinic and legal sources made him a standing check on the divines' claims for church government by divine right. The History of Tithes (1618) was suppressed and forced a submission from him. De Diis Syris (1617) and De Jure Naturali et Gentium juxta Disciplinam Ebraeorum (1640) built his European reputation. Table Talk, compiled by his secretary and printed in 1689, preserves the conversational voice.

John Strickland.bio: One of the ministers named to the Westminster Assembly. His public significance rests on that membership and on a small number of sermons preached before Parliament in the 1640s and printed at its order; nothing further is asserted here.

John Wallis.tradition: Church of England; served the Westminster Assembly as a scribe
John Wallis.affiliation: Savilian Professor of Geometry, University of Oxford
John Wallis.bio: Wallis served as a scribe to the Westminster Assembly and as a cipher-breaker for Parliament before he was given the Savilian chair of geometry at Oxford in 1649, which he held until his death. Arithmetica Infinitorum (1656) laid groundwork Newton later drew on, and Wallis introduced the lemniscate as the sign for infinity. He was a founding member of the Royal Society, wrote a grammar of English, worked at teaching the deaf to speak, and defended the doctrine of the Trinity against Socinian critics in the 1690s.

John Ward.bio: One of the ministers named to the Westminster Assembly. The name is common enough in seventeenth-century English church records that no dates, living or publications are attached to him here.

John Whincop.bio: A member of the Westminster Assembly, known chiefly for that membership and for a sermon preached before the House of Commons in the mid-1640s and printed at the House's order.

John White.affiliation: Rector of Holy Trinity, Dorchester; assessor of the Westminster Assembly
John White.bio: White was rector at Dorchester for some forty years and was called the Patriarch of Dorchester for the programme of civic and religious reform he ran in the town. He promoted English settlement in New England, helped organise the Dorchester Company and the venture that became the Massachusetts Bay Company, and defended the project in The Planters Plea (1630). Parliament named him to the Westminster Assembly, where he served as one of its assessors. He should not be confused with the lawyer John White, the MP who chaired the Commons committee on scandalous ministers.

Joseph Caryl.affiliation: Preacher to Lincoln's Inn; member of the Westminster Assembly
Joseph Caryl.bio: Caryl was preacher to Lincoln's Inn and a member of the Westminster Assembly, and Parliament used him repeatedly as an attending minister, including at Holdenby with the captive king and with Cromwell's army in Scotland. He is remembered for one work of extraordinary scale: an exposition of Job preached and published in instalments from 1644 to 1666, running to twelve quarto volumes and standing among the longest commentaries on a single book in English. Ejected in 1662, he gathered an Independent congregation in London that was united with John Owen's after his death.

Joseph Hall.affiliation: Bishop of Exeter, then of Norwich; English delegate to the Synod of Dort
Joseph Hall.bio: Hall began as a verse satirist with Virgidemiarum (1597 and 1598) and ended as a bishop stripped of his revenues. He represented the Church of England at the Synod of Dort in 1618, held Exeter from 1627 and Norwich from 1641, and was briefly imprisoned with the bishops who protested their exclusion from the Lords. His Humble Remonstrance (1641) for episcopacy drew the Smectymnuus reply and then Milton's. Meditations and Vows, The Art of Divine Meditation and Heaven upon Earth made him the first English Protestant to teach a systematic method of meditation.

Joshua Hoyle.affiliation: Regius Professor of Divinity, Oxford; Master of University College; member of the Westminster Assembly
Joshua Hoyle.bio: Hoyle taught divinity at Trinity College, Dublin, until the Irish rebellion of 1641 drove him to England. He sat in the Westminster Assembly, and the parliamentary visitors installed him at Oxford as Master of University College and Regius Professor of Divinity, where he remained until his death in 1654. He published little, and what there is belongs to anti-Roman controversy rather than constructive theology. His interest for a reader here is as a link between the Dublin divinity of Ussher's circle and the Assembly's benches.

Josias Simmler.affiliation: Professor of theology at the Zurich Carolinum
Josias Simmler.bio: Simler taught at the Zurich Carolinum, first on the New Testament and then, after Peter Martyr Vermigli's death in 1562, in his chair of theology. De aeterno Dei Filio (1568) defended the eternal deity of the Son against the Italian antitrinitarians who had taken refuge in Poland and Transylvania, and is the fullest Reformed Trinitarian statement of that generation. He also wrote lives of Bullinger and of Vermigli, worked on Conrad Gessner's Bibliotheca universalis, and produced De Alpibus commentarius (1574), among the earliest descriptive accounts of the Alps.

Juan José Urráburu.affiliation: Professor of philosophy, Pontifical Gregorian University, Rome
Juan José Urráburu.bio: Urráburu was a Spanish Jesuit who taught philosophy in Rome during the neo-scholastic revival that followed Leo XIII's encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879). His Institutiones Philosophicae, issued in eight large Latin volumes from 1890, is among the most extensive philosophy courses of the period, covering logic, cosmology, psychology, natural theology and ethics in scholastic order; a shorter Compendium followed for classroom use. He is read now mainly by historians of nineteenth-century Thomism and of the Suarezian strand within the Jesuit schools.

Juan de Torquemada.affiliation: Cardinal; Master of the Sacred Palace; theologian at the Councils of Basel and Ferrara-Florence
Juan de Torquemada.bio: Torquemada was a Castilian Dominican who argued the papal case at Basel and then at Ferrara-Florence, where he had a hand in the decree of union with the Greeks, and who was made a cardinal in 1439. His Summa de Ecclesia, finished in 1453, is the fullest fifteenth-century defence of papal primacy against conciliarism and became a quarry for Counter-Reformation controversialists. He also wrote in defence of converts from Judaism against the blood-purity statutes of Toledo. He was the uncle of Tomás de Torquemada, the inquisitor, and is often confused with him.

Lancelot Andrewes.affiliation: Dean of Westminster; Bishop of Chichester, then Ely, then Winchester
Lancelot Andrewes.bio: Andrewes was Dean of Westminster from 1601 and afterward bishop of Chichester, Ely and Winchester in turn, and he directed the First Westminster company that translated Genesis through Second Kings for the King James Bible. James I set him to answer Bellarmine on the oath of allegiance, which he did in the Responsio of 1610. The XCVI Sermons, gathered by Laud and Buckeridge in 1629, are the monument of his preaching, dense with patristic citation and word-by-word exposition. The Preces Privatae, his Greek and Latin private devotions, were never meant for print.

Lazarus Seaman.affiliation: Master of Peterhouse, Cambridge; member of the Westminster Assembly
Lazarus Seaman.bio: Seaman was a Presbyterian member of the Westminster Assembly and one of its more active speakers on church government. Parliament made him Master of Peterhouse, Cambridge, in 1644, and he served a term as vice-chancellor of the university. He lost both posts and his London living at the Restoration and afterward preached to a gathered congregation. He published sermons and controversial pieces rather than a system, so his standing rests on the Assembly's debates. The sale of his library in 1676 is usually counted the first book auction held in England.

Leonard Lessius.affiliation: Professor of theology, Jesuit college at Louvain
Leonard Lessius.bio: Lessius taught theology at the Jesuit college in Louvain from 1585 and was drawn at once into controversy: propositions on grace and predestination drawn from his lectures were censured by the Louvain and Douai faculties in 1587, an episode that fed the De auxiliis dispute with the Dominicans. De iustitia et iure (1605) is his lasting work, a treatise on contracts, interest, insurance and just price that later historians of economic thought read closely. He also wrote De providentia numinis against unbelief, and devotional works on the names of God.

Leopoldus Dorn.bio: A Latinised form of a German name, of the kind early modern academic and clerical writers used on title pages. Nothing further is asserted here.

Libert Froidmont.tradition: Roman Catholic; Augustinian current at Louvain
Libert Froidmont.affiliation: Professor of Sacred Scripture, University of Louvain
Libert Froidmont.bio: Froidmont, who wrote as Fromondus, held chairs of philosophy and then of Sacred Scripture at Louvain, where he was the close friend of Cornelius Jansen. After Jansen's death he saw the Augustinus through the press in 1640, the book that gave Jansenism its name and its text. His own writing ran to natural philosophy as much as divinity: the Meteorologicorum libri sex, and the Anti-Aristarchus of 1631 against the motion of the earth, which put him in correspondence and disagreement with Descartes and Gassendi. He also published commentaries on the Pauline epistles.

Lucas Lossius.bio: Lossius studied under Melanchthon at Wittenberg and then spent his working life as a schoolmaster in Lüneburg. His Psalmodia, hoc est cantica sacra veteris ecclesiae selecta (1553) gathered the Latin chant of the medieval offices with Lutheran adaptation, and is a principal witness to how much of the old liturgy the early Lutheran schools went on singing. He also produced textbooks in rhetoric, dialectic and grammar, and annotations on the New Testament. He matters to anyone tracing liturgical continuity across the Reformation rather than rupture.

Ludwig Lavater.bio: Lavater was a Zurich minister, Bullinger's son-in-law, and from 1585 antistes of the Zurich church in his turn. He wrote commentaries on Old Testament books, an account of the rites and observances of the Zurich church, and a life of Bullinger. Outside the Reformed world he is known for De spectris, lemuribus et magnis atque insolitis fragoribus (1569), englished as Of Ghostes and Spirites Walking by Nyght, which argued that apparitions are natural or diabolical rather than the returning dead, and which readers of Hamlet have long had reason to consult.

Martin Chemnitz.affiliation: Superintendent of the church at Braunschweig
Martin Chemnitz.bio: Chemnitz was superintendent at Braunschweig from 1567 and the chief systematiser of Lutheran theology after Luther's death, so much so that the old tag ran that if the second Martin had not come, the first would not have stood. The Examen Concilii Tridentini (1565 to 1573) takes Trent decree by decree and remains the standard Lutheran answer to it. De duabus naturis in Christo (1570) set out the christology of the communication of attributes, and with Andreae and Selnecker he was a principal author of the Formula of Concord (1577). His Loci Theologici were published posthumously.

Matthew Newcomen.affiliation: Minister at Dedham, Essex; member of the Westminster Assembly
Matthew Newcomen.bio: Newcomen was lecturer and then minister at Dedham in Essex for some thirty years and a member of the Westminster Assembly.
