He supplied the N in Smectymnuus, the acronym of the five Presbyterian ministers whose Answer to Joseph Hall's Humble Remonstrance opened the episcopacy controversy of 1641 and brought Milton in on their side. He preached before Parliament in the 1640s. Ejected in 1662, he took a pastorate among the English congregation at Leiden and died there of the plague.

Matthew Poole.affiliation: Rector of St Michael le Querne, London, until 1662
Matthew Poole.bio: Poole held a London living until the Act of Uniformity put him out in 1662, and then spent a decade on the Synopsis Criticorum (1669 to 1676), five folio volumes digesting the Protestant and Catholic biblical commentators of the previous century into one running apparatus. It is a labour of compression rather than of original exegesis, and it is why he is still on shelves. The English Annotations upon the Holy Bible, completed by other hands after his death, carried the same method to a wider readership. He died at Amsterdam, having fled the Popish Plot.

Matthias Martini.affiliation: Rector of the Gymnasium Illustre, Bremen
Matthias Martini.bio: Martini taught at Herborn before going to Bremen, where he led the Gymnasium Illustre from 1610. He headed the Bremen delegation to the Synod of Dort, where he and his colleagues pressed a broader construction of the death of Christ than the Contra-Remonstrant majority wanted; the friction was open enough to leave traces in the proceedings, and he signed the canons in the end. His Lexicon Philologicum (1623) served as a standard etymological dictionary of Latin for a century, and his covenant theology fed the later federal tradition.

Melchior Leydekker.affiliation: Professor of theology, University of Utrecht
Melchior Leydekker.bio: Leydekker held a chair of theology at Utrecht from 1678 and was a leading voice of the Voetian party in its long quarrel with the Cocceians over covenant theology and the Sabbath, and with the Cartesians over the place of philosophy in divinity. Fax veritatis (1677) and De veritate religionis reformatae are the works usually cited. He also wrote on the history of the church in the Netherlands and on the Jansenist controversy. He belongs to the late Dutch orthodoxy that codified and defended what Dort had settled.

Moïse Amyraut.affiliation: Professor of theology, Protestant Academy of Saumur
Moïse Amyraut.bio: Amyraut taught at the Academy of Saumur from 1633 and developed the teaching of his master John Cameron into what took his name: a decree of universal conditional redemption standing logically before the decree of election, so that Christ died for all hypothetically and for the elect effectually. The Brief traitté de la predestination (1634) brought charges of heterodoxy, and the national synods of Alençon in 1637 and Charenton in 1644 heard and acquitted him. He also wrote on Christian ethics, on the epistles, and in defence of Huguenot loyalty to the French crown.

Oliver Bowles.affiliation: Rector of Sutton, Bedfordshire; member of the Westminster Assembly
Oliver Bowles.bio: An aged English minister, rector of Sutton in Bedfordshire, who was named to the Westminster Assembly and preached at the fast kept for its opening in July 1643, a sermon printed as Zeale for Gods House Quickned. His one substantial book, De pastore evangelico tractatus, is a Latin treatise on the pastoral office covering the minister's calling, study, preaching and discipline, and it belongs with the Puritan literature on the ministry that Baxter's Reformed Pastor later made familiar. His birth and death years are not securely fixed and are left out here.

Paolo Sarpi.affiliation: Theologian and canonist to the Republic of Venice
Paolo Sarpi.bio: A Servite friar of Venice who became the Republic's official theologian and canonist and defended Venetian jurisdiction against Paul V through the interdict of 1606 and 1607, surviving an attempt on his life in the aftermath. He is read chiefly for the Istoria del Concilio Tridentino, printed at London in 1619 under the name Pietro Soave Polano, which presents Trent as a work of curial management rather than of the Spirit. Pallavicino's history was commissioned against it, and the two are still read as a pair. Sarpi also corresponded with Protestant scholars and worked in anatomy and optics.

Paul Laymann.affiliation: Professor of moral theology at Munich; professor of canon law at Dillingen
Paul Laymann.bio: A Jesuit born near Innsbruck who taught philosophy at Ingolstadt, moral theology in the Jesuit college at Munich, and canon law at Dillingen. His Theologia moralis, first printed in 1625, became one of the standard casuistical manuals of the seventeenth century and was reissued for well over a hundred years; he wrote also on canon law and on the jurisdiction of religious superiors. A reader meets him wherever post-Tridentine moral theology is being cited, whether by Catholic casuists building on him or by Protestant controversialists attacking the casuistry of the schools.

Paul Lazarus.bio: This name cannot be identified with confidence, and nothing is asserted about the person here.

Peter Smith.bio: An English name too common to identify securely; no dates, office or works are asserted here.

Pierre Grégoire (Tholosanus).affiliation: Professor of law at Toulouse, Cahors and Pont-à-Mousson
Pierre Grégoire (Tholosanus).bio: A French civil lawyer known by the Latin byname Tholosanus, after his native Toulouse, where he studied and taught before holding chairs at Cahors and at the university of Pont-à-Mousson in Lorraine. His Syntagma iuris universi attempted a systematic ordering of the whole of law, and De republica libri sex et viginti set out a theory of political authority in the generation of Bodin. He is cited in later arguments over the origin of civil power and the relation of magistracy to divine and natural law, which is how he turns up in confessional political writing.

Pierre Viret.affiliation: Reformer of Lausanne and teacher in its academy; later minister in France and in Béarn
Pierre Viret.bio: Born at Orbe in the Pays de Vaud and won to the Reformation by Guillaume Farel, Viret led the reform of Lausanne after the Bernese conquest of 1536 and taught in its academy until he was expelled in 1559 in the quarrel with Bern over discipline and excommunication. His last years were spent preaching in France, at Nîmes, Montpellier and Lyon, and finally in Béarn under Jeanne d'Albret. His vernacular dialogues and works of instruction, among them the Disputations chrestiennes, made him one of the most widely read French-speaking reformers of his own lifetime.

Pietro Maria Gazzaniga.affiliation: Professor of dogmatic theology, University of Vienna
Pietro Maria Gazzaniga.bio: An Italian Dominican who taught dogmatic theology at Vienna under Maria Theresa and Joseph II. His Praelectiones theologicae, issued in many volumes and often reprinted, gave a Thomist dogmatics set against the Jansenist and Febronian currents then strong in the Habsburg lands. He is met mainly as a manualist, a witness to how Catholic school theology stated the questions of grace, the church and papal authority in the later eighteenth century, just before the upheaval of the revolutionary years.

Pietro Sforza Pallavicino.affiliation: Professor at the Collegio Romano; cardinal from 1659
Pietro Sforza Pallavicino.bio: A Roman nobleman who entered the Society of Jesus in 1637, taught philosophy and then theology at the Collegio Romano, and was made cardinal by Alexander VII in 1659. He is read for the Istoria del Concilio di Trento, published in 1656 and 1657, written at Roman direction to answer Sarpi out of the conciliar archives and the papers of the legates. The two histories are still worked through against each other, Sarpi as the hostile insider and Pallavicino with access to documents Sarpi never saw. He also wrote on rhetoric and moral philosophy.

Raimundus de Sabunde.bio: A theologian of Catalan origin who taught at Toulouse, where he is recorded as a master of arts, medicine and theology. His one surviving work, written in the 1430s and known as the Liber creaturarum or Theologia naturalis, argues from the book of creatures to the articles of the faith, treating nature and Scripture as two books given by one author. It reached a wide readership through Montaigne, who translated it at his father's request and then wrote the Apologie de Raimond Sebond, turning the book's confidence in natural reason into an occasion for skepticism.

Remigius Bäumer (Hrsg.).affiliation: Professor of church history, University of Freiburg im Breisgau
Remigius Bäumer (Hrsg.).bio: Not an early modern author but the modern editor named on the title page; Hrsg. is the German abbreviation for Herausgeber, editor. Bäumer was a German Catholic church historian at Freiburg im Breisgau who edited collections of scholarship on conciliarism, the papacy and the Reformation era, including volumes in the Wege der Forschung series that gather the standard essays on the councils of the fifteenth century and on Luther's Catholic opponents. What stands under his name here is a compilation of texts or studies rather than a work of his own composition.

Richard Baxter.affiliation: Lecturer and pastor at Kidderminster; chaplain in the parliamentary army
Richard Baxter.bio: Baxter was never a university man. He served Kidderminster from 1641, apart from an interval as chaplain to a parliamentary regiment, and made that parish the working model of the catechizing discipline set out in The Reformed Pastor of 1656. At the Restoration he declined the see of Hereford, argued for comprehension at the Savoy Conference of 1661, and was ejected in 1662; he was tried before Jeffreys in 1685. The Saints Everlasting Rest, A Christian Directory and the posthumous Reliquiae Baxterianae carry his practical divinity, his casuistry and his own account of the age.

Richard Field.affiliation: Dean of Gloucester; chaplain to Elizabeth I and James I
Richard Field.bio: An Oxford-trained divine who lectured in divinity at Lincoln's Inn, served as chaplain to Elizabeth I and then to James I, and held the deanery of Gloucester from 1609. His Of the Church, in five books published between 1606 and 1610, is the fullest English treatment of the doctrine of the church in the generation after Hooker, arguing that the Church of England stands within the catholic church while Rome has corrupted what it claims to guard. Field knew Hooker, and the two are commonly read together on the marks and identity of the church.

Richard Heyrick.tradition: Presbyterian, within the Church of England
Richard Heyrick.affiliation: Warden of the Collegiate Church, Manchester; member of the Westminster Assembly
Richard Heyrick.bio: Warden of the collegiate church at Manchester from 1635 and a leader of the Lancashire Presbyterians, Heyrick sat in the Westminster Assembly and helped organize the county's classical presbyteries, the most fully working presbyterian system England actually achieved. He subscribed the Harmonious Consent of the Lancashire ministers in 1648 and opposed the execution of the king; suspicion of a hand in Christopher Love's plot brought him imprisonment in 1651. He kept the wardenship through the Interregnum and into the Restoration.

Richard Hooker.affiliation: Master of the Temple; rector of Bishopsbourne, Kent
Richard Hooker.bio: Educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, Hooker was Master of the Temple from 1585, where his morning sermons were answered each afternoon by the presbyterian lecturer Walter Travers, and afterwards held country livings, ending at Bishopsbourne in Kent. Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, whose first four books appeared in 1593 and the fifth in 1597, defends the English settlement by an argument about law, reason and the church's authority in things indifferent rather than by an exchange of proof texts. The last three books were printed after his death and their text has been contested ever since.

Richard Sibbes.affiliation: Preacher at Gray's Inn; Master of St Catharine's Hall, Cambridge
Richard Sibbes.bio: A Cambridge man who held the lectureship at Holy Trinity, Cambridge until he lost it in the mid 1610s, then preached to the lawyers at Gray's Inn in London from 1617 and from 1626 held the mastership of St Catharine's Hall alongside that lectureship. He was one of the Feoffees for Impropriations, the Puritan trust that bought up livings until Laud broke it in 1633. The Bruised Reed and Smoking Flax and The Souls Conflict with Itself are the works he is read for, mild in temper and aimed at the doubting conscience rather than at controversy.

Richard Vines.affiliation: Master of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge; member of the Westminster Assembly
Richard Vines.bio: One of the more effective speakers in the Westminster Assembly, where he argued the Presbyterian case against the Dissenting Brethren on church government and against the Erastians on the power of the keys. He was Master of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge from 1644 until his removal in 1650 for refusing the Engagement to the Commonwealth, and afterwards held St Lawrence Jewry in London. He attended the parliamentary commissioners in the treaty negotiations with Charles I and preached often before Parliament; his printed sermons and a treatise on the Lord's Supper are what survive of his work.

Robert Baillie.affiliation: Professor of Divinity and later Principal, University of Glasgow; Scottish commissioner to the Westminster Assembly
Robert Baillie.bio: A minister of Kilwinning who went to London in 1643 as one of the Scottish commissioners to the Westminster Assembly and remained for most of its work. His Letters and Journals, printed long after his death, are the nearest thing to a running record of the Assembly and of Covenanting politics, candid about the Independents and about his own side. He wrote against the sects in A Dissuasive from the Errours of the Time in 1645, held the divinity chair at Glasgow from 1642, and was made Principal there at the Restoration.

Rodrigo de Arriaga.affiliation: Professor of theology and chancellor, University of Prague
Rodrigo de Arriaga.bio: A Spanish Jesuit who spent most of his life in Bohemia, teaching theology at Prague and serving as chancellor of the university there. His Cursus philosophicus of 1632 was read across Europe and made him one of the recognized names of late scholasticism, and his Disputationes theologicae ran to eight folio volumes. He is met in the arguments over grace and free will, where he stands with the Jesuits against the Dominican account, and in the seventeenth century disputes over matter, place and quantity that Protestant scholastics were working through at the same time.

Rudolf Gwalther.affiliation: Antistes of the Zurich church from 1575
Rudolf Gwalther.bio: Raised in Zurich within Zwingli's circle and married to Zwingli's daughter Regula, Gwalther edited and translated Zwingli's works into Latin and succeeded Bullinger as Antistes, head of the Zurich church, in 1575. His long series of Latin homilies on the New Testament books were printed and reprinted for readers on the continent and in England, and Der Endchrist of 1546 set out the Zurich case that the papacy is the Antichrist. Through a heavy correspondence with England he is one of the channels by which Zurich divinity reached the Elizabethan church.

Samuel Gibson.bio: An English minister who appears among the divines named to the Westminster Assembly. Nothing further is asserted here, as his dates, livings and any published work cannot be stated with confidence.

Samuel Rutherford.affiliation: Minister of Anwoth; Professor of Divinity and Principal of St Mary's College, St Andrews; Scottish commissioner to the Westminster Assembly
Samuel Rutherford.bio: Minister of Anwoth in Galloway from 1627 until the Court of High Commission confined him at Aberdeen in 1636, where he wrote most of the letters gathered in 1664 as Joshua Redivivus. He served as a Scottish commissioner at Westminster, then took the divinity chair at St Andrews and the principalship of St Mary's College in 1647. Lex, Rex of 1644 argues that the king holds his power from the people under law and that resistance may be lawful; it was burned at the Restoration and he was summoned for treason, dying before he could answer.

Sebastian Schmid.affiliation: Professor of Old Testament, University of Strasbourg
Sebastian Schmid.bio: A Lutheran Hebraist who taught at Strasbourg for most of his career and commented on much of the Old Testament and parts of the New. He is remembered above all for a strictly literal Latin version of the Bible, printed at the end of his life, which held close to Hebrew and Greek word order at the cost of elegance and served later exegetes, Bengel among them, as a working text. He belongs to the last stretch of Lutheran orthodoxy, just before Pietism reshaped German biblical study.

Sidrach Simpson.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; Master of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge
Sidrach Simpson.bio: One of the five Dissenting Brethren at the Westminster Assembly, with Thomas Goodwin, Philip Nye, Jeremiah Burroughes and William Bridge, whose Apologeticall Narration of 1644 carried the case for congregational independency to the reading public rather than to the Assembly floor. Simpson had pastored an English congregation in the Netherlands during the Laudian years, returned to a gathered church in London, and was made Master of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge in 1650. He is read for the Independent side of the Assembly's debates on church government and toleration.

Simeon Ashe.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; chaplain to the Earl of Manchester
Simeon Ashe.bio: A Presbyterian silenced for nonconformity under Laud, afterwards chaplain to the Earl of Manchester in the parliamentary army and a member of the Westminster Assembly. In London he held a city living and became known for funeral sermons on his fellow ministers and for bringing other men's Puritan manuscripts to the press with prefaces of his own. He opposed the execution of the king and worked for the Presbyterian settlement that the Restoration undid, dying in August 1662 in the days around the ejection of the nonconforming clergy.

Stanislaus Hosius.affiliation: Bishop of Ermland; cardinal; papal legate presiding at the Council of Trent, 1562–1563
Stanislaus Hosius.bio: A Polish churchman, bishop of Ermland from 1551 and cardinal from 1561, who presided as one of the papal legates over the closing sessions of Trent in 1562 and 1563. His Confessio fidei catholicae Christiana of 1553, drawn up for a Polish synod, went through many editions and became one of the standard Catholic statements against the Reformation; Protestant controversialists were still answering it a century later. He brought the Jesuits into Poland, founding their college at Braunsberg in 1564, and is generally credited with checking the Protestant advance there.

Stanley Gower.bio: A member of the Westminster Assembly who had served as chaplain to Sir Robert Harley at Brampton Bryan in Herefordshire before the war and who preached before the House of Commons at one of its fast days. Little else can be stated with confidence, so no dates or further livings are given here.

Stephen Charnock.affiliation: Fellow of New College, Oxford; chaplain to Henry Cromwell in Ireland; co-pastor at Crosby Hall, London
Stephen Charnock.bio: Educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge and made a fellow of New College, Oxford under the parliamentary visitation, Charnock went to Ireland as chaplain to Henry Cromwell and lost the place at the Restoration. He preached privately for years before joining Thomas Watson as co-pastor of a Presbyterian congregation at Crosby Hall in London in 1675. The Existence and Attributes of God, assembled from his sermons and printed in 1682 after his death, is the work he is read for, a sustained and closely argued treatment of the divine perfections.

Synod of Dort.affiliation: National synod of the Dutch Reformed churches, Dordrecht
Synod of Dort.bio: A national synod of the Dutch Reformed churches, sitting at Dordrecht from November 1618 to May 1619, with voting delegates invited from Britain, the Palatinate, Hesse, Switzerland, Geneva, Bremen and Emden. The French delegation was forbidden to travel by Louis XIII. The States General called it to settle the quarrel raised by the Remonstrance of 1610, and it condemned the Remonstrant articles in the Canons of Dort, five heads of doctrine treating corruption, election, the death of Christ, grace and perseverance. The synod also deposed Remonstrant ministers, endorsed the Belgic Confession and Heidelberg Catechism, and commissioned the Dutch States Bible.

Theodore Beza.affiliation: Rector of the Academy of Geneva; moderator of the Venerable Company of Pastors
Theodore Beza.bio: French humanist and lawyer who broke with Rome in 1548, taught Greek at Lausanne, and succeeded Calvin at Geneva in 1564. He led the Company of Pastors, presided over the Academy, and spoke for the French Reformed at the Colloquy of Poissy in 1561. His editions of the Greek New Testament, with Latin translation and annotations, shaped the Geneva and King James renderings, and Codex Bezae carries his name. He is read for the Tabula praedestinationis (1555), for his life of Calvin, and for De iure magistratuum (1574), which defends resistance by lesser magistrates after the St Bartholomew's Day massacre.

Thomas Bedford.affiliation: Rector of St Martin Outwich, London
Thomas Bedford.bio: Cambridge-trained clergyman who studied under John Davenant and Samuel Ward and served as rector of St Martin Outwich in London. He wrote chiefly on the sacraments and on the efficacy of baptism, in A Treatise of the Sacrament (1638), Some Sacramental Instructions (1649) and Vindiciae Gratiae Sacramentalis (1650), holding a high view of baptismal grace that drew the charge of Arminianism from other Calvinists and a reply from Richard Baxter, who later published a friendly accommodation with him in 1656. His Examination of some of the Chief Points of Antinomianism (1647) came out of lectures given at St Antholine's.

Thomas Brooks.affiliation: Minister of St Margaret's, Fish Street Hill, London
Thomas Brooks.bio: Puritan preacher who served as a chaplain at sea during the civil wars, then settled in London at St Thomas Apostle and afterwards at St Margaret's, Fish Street Hill. He was ejected in 1662 and stayed in the city through the plague and the fire, preaching where he could. He is read for compact devotional works, above all Precious Remedies against Satan's Devices (1652), which catalogues temptations one by one and sets an answer against each, and for The Mute Christian under the Smarting Rod, Heaven on Earth, and Apples of Gold for Young Men and Women.

Thomas Carter.bio: One of the ministers summoned to the Westminster Assembly in 1643. Almost nothing beyond that membership is recoverable, and he is readily confused with William Carter and with John Carter, both of whom left more of a record.

Thomas Coleman.affiliation: Rector of Blyton, Lincolnshire; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Coleman.bio: Hebraist whose learning earned him the name Rabbi Coleman. He left his Lincolnshire rectory in 1642 under pressure from royalist troops and came to London, where he sat in the Westminster Assembly as the clerical leader of its Erastian minority, arguing with John Selden and John Lightfoot that the power of church censures rests finally with the civil magistrate. His sermon before Parliament in 1645 drew a reply from George Gillespie, and the exchange ran on through several pamphlets, including A Brotherly Examination Re-examined, until Coleman died in March 1647.

Thomas Ford.affiliation: Minister at Exeter; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Ford.bio: Expelled from Magdalen Hall, Oxford, in 1631 for a sermon against Arminian teaching, he spent the following years in the Netherlands before returning to England, sitting in the Westminster Assembly and settling at Exeter. He was ejected in 1662 and preached privately in the city until his death. What survives of him is sermons rather than a system, including fast sermons preached to Parliament and a defence of the singing of psalms as a Christian duty.

Thomas Goodwin.affiliation: President of Magdalen College, Oxford; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Goodwin.bio: Cambridge preacher who left the ceremonies of the established church for the Independent way and pastored an English congregation at Arnhem, then returned to sit in the Westminster Assembly. There he was one of the five authors of An Apologeticall Narration (1643), which pressed the congregational case before Parliament. Cromwell made him President of Magdalen College, Oxford, and he helped frame the Savoy Declaration of 1658. He is read for his expositions of Ephesians and Revelation, for The Heart of Christ in Heaven towards Sinners on Earth, and for A Child of Light Walking in Darkness.

Thomas Hill.affiliation: Master of Trinity College, Cambridge; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Hill.bio: Herefordshire man educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, who sat in the Westminster Assembly from 1643 and was placed by Parliament first over Emmanuel and then over Trinity College, serving as Master of Trinity from 1645 until his death and as Vice-Chancellor of the university in 1646. What survives of him is chiefly the fast sermons he preached to the Long Parliament, printed as The Trade of Truth Advanced and The Militant Church Triumphant over the Dragon, together with university and funeral sermons.

Thomas Manton.affiliation: Rector of St Paul's, Covent Garden; chaplain to Charles II
Thomas Manton.bio: Devon-born preacher who lectured at Stoke Newington before moving to St Paul's, Covent Garden. He worked for a comprehensive church settlement at the Restoration, served briefly as a royal chaplain, took part in the Savoy Conference of 1661, was ejected the next year, and was later imprisoned for preaching. He is read for expository preaching in bulk, above all one hundred and ninety sermons on Psalm 119, and for commentaries on James and Jude. The epistle to the reader in the 1658 edition of the Westminster Confession is commonly attributed to him.

Thomas Temple.affiliation: Rector of Battersea, Surrey; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Temple.bio: Minister at Winwick in Northamptonshire and then at Battersea in Surrey, named to the Westminster Assembly in 1643 and reported to have attended steadily, and appointed one of the licensers of divinity books for the press. He preached before the Commons at their public fast on 26 October 1642, printed as Christ's Government in and over his People. Reference works give his dates inconsistently, so none are stated here.

Thomas Thorowgood.affiliation: Rector of Grimston, Norfolk; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Thorowgood.bio: Norfolk clergyman named to the Westminster Assembly in 1643 and said to have attended it constantly, later placed by Parliament in the rectory of Crayford in Kent. He is remembered less for the Assembly than for Iewes in America, or, Probabilities that the Americans are of that Race (1650), written with encouragement from John Dury, which argued that the native peoples of America descend from the ten tribes and pressed English readers to support missions among them. An enlarged edition of 1660 leans on the work of John Eliot.

Thomas Valentine.affiliation: Rector of Chalfont St Giles, Buckinghamshire; member of the Westminster Assembly
Thomas Valentine.bio: Rector of Chalfont St Giles who was in trouble with the church courts under Laud before the civil wars and sat in the Westminster Assembly from 1643. He was ejected in 1662 and went on gathering his people for worship at the Vache, the Buckinghamshire house of Charles Fleetwood. Little of his preaching reached print, and his public standing rests on that Assembly membership rather than on a body of published work.

Thomas Watson.affiliation: Rector of St Stephen Walbrook, London
Thomas Watson.bio: London minister at St Stephen Walbrook, imprisoned in 1651 for his part in Christopher Love's plot to bring in Charles II, and ejected in 1662. He afterwards preached in a hall in Bishopsgate, for a time with Stephen Charnock. He is read for plain and aphoristic writing rather than for controversy: A Body of Divinity, which follows the questions of the Westminster Shorter Catechism, The Doctrine of Repentance, The Art of Divine Contentment, and his exposition of the Beatitudes. He is among the most quotable of the Puritan writers and the least technical.

Thomas Westfield.affiliation: Bishop of Bristol; Archdeacon of St Albans
Thomas Westfield.bio: Long the preacher at St Bartholomew the Great in London, and made Bishop of Bristol in 1642 as the crown tried to fill vacant sees with men of moderate reputation. He was named to the Westminster Assembly in the parliamentary ordinance of 1643, but like the other bishops summoned he never took his place, and he died the following year. His printed remains are sermons, gathered and published after his death.

Thomas Young.affiliation: Vicar of Stowmarket, Suffolk; Master of Jesus College, Cambridge
Thomas Young.bio: Scot educated at St Andrews who tutored the young John Milton, served the English merchant congregation at Hamburg, and held the vicarage of Stowmarket in Suffolk. He supplied the initials TY in Smectymnuus, the composite name of the five Presbyterian ministers whose answer to Joseph Hall in 1641 argued against episcopacy, and he is usually taken to have drafted much of it. He sat in the Westminster Assembly, was made Master of Jesus College, Cambridge, in 1644, and lost the post for refusing the Engagement.

Tilemann Heshusius.affiliation: Professor of theology at Rostock, Heidelberg, Jena and Helmstedt
Tilemann Heshusius.bio: Westphalian theologian trained under Melanchthon at Wittenberg who spent his career on the strict Lutheran side of every quarrel and was removed from one post after another. As general superintendent in the Palatinate he fought the deacon Wilhelm Klebitz over the Lord's Supper, and Frederick III dismissed them both in 1559, a step on the road to the Heidelberg Catechism. Calvin answered him in the Dilucida explicatio of 1561. He taught afterwards at Jena and from 1577 at Helmstedt, where he declined to subscribe the Formula of Concord over its teaching on the communication of attributes.

Walter Brandmüller.affiliation: President of the Pontifical Committee for Historical Sciences from 1998; Cardinal
Walter Brandmüller.bio: German church historian, long a professor at Augsburg, whose scholarly subject is the history of the ecumenical councils, above all Constance (1414–1418) and Basel. He founded the journal Annuarium Historiae Conciliorum and edits the Konziliengeschichte series, which supplies much of the modern apparatus for conciliar documents. He was appointed president of the Pontifical Committee for Historical Sciences in 1998 and created cardinal by Benedict XVI in 2010. In this library his name attaches to editions and studies of council material rather than to a source from the period.

Willem Hessels van Est.affiliation: Professor of theology and chancellor of the University of Douai
Willem Hessels van Est.bio: Known in Latin as Estius. Born at Gorinchem in Holland, he taught at Douai from 1580 and became chancellor of the university there. His commentary on the Pauline epistles, In omnes divi Pauli epistolas commentaria, was read for centuries by Catholics and Protestants alike for its plain grammatical exegesis. His commentary on the Sentences of Peter Lombard is strongly Augustinian on grace, close enough to the Louvain school to attract suspicion during the Jansenist controversies that followed. He also wrote the account of the Martyrs of Gorkum, among whom were his own kinsmen. This library carries his name twice, here and as Willem van Est.

Willem van Est.affiliation: Professor of theology and chancellor of the University of Douai
Willem van Est.bio: A shorter form of the name of Willem Hessels van Est, the Douai exegete known in Latin as Estius. The library carries both spellings, so this entry and the entry under Willem Hessels van Est are one man and not two: the professor and chancellor at Douai who commented on the Pauline epistles and on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, and whose reading of Augustine on grace was later argued over in the Jansenist disputes. See that entry for the fuller account.

William Bucanus.affiliation: Professor of theology at the Academy of Lausanne
William Bucanus.bio: Guillaume Du Buc, a French-speaking Swiss Reformed pastor at Yverdon from 1571 and professor of theology at Lausanne from 1591. His Institutiones theologicae (Geneva, 1602) sets out the whole of doctrine as a series of questions and answers, taken topic by topic, and it became a standard teaching text. Robert Hill's English version appeared in 1606 as Institutions of Christian Religion and circulated later as A Body of Divinity. Readers meet him here as an example of early Reformed scholastic method, before the fuller systems of the seventeenth century.

William Carter.bio: London preacher educated at Cambridge who sat in the Westminster Assembly among its small group of Independents, the men Robert Baillie named alongside Thomas Goodwin, Philip Nye, Jeremiah Burroughs and William Bridge. Assembly records place him there from 1643. He left little in print, and his public significance is that membership and the congregational side he took in the debates over church government.

William Chillingworth.bio: Oxford scholar and godson of William Laud who was argued into the Roman church by the Jesuit John Fisher, went to the English college at Douai, and then returned to the Church of England. The Religion of Protestants a Safe Way to Salvation (1638) is his answer to Catholic claims of infallible authority, resting on the sufficiency and clarity of Scripture and on the modest certainty available to honest inquiry. The much quoted sentence that the Bible only is the religion of Protestants is his. He served the royalist army as an engineer, was taken at Arundel in 1643, and died at Chichester, harried to the end by Francis Cheynell.

William Perkins.affiliation: Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge; lecturer at Great St Andrew's, Cambridge
William Perkins.bio: English theologian whose books were reprinted and translated across Protestant Europe. He lectured at Great St Andrew's in Cambridge and worked out a practical divinity aimed at the conscience: A Golden Chaine (1590), with its chart of the order of the causes of salvation, The Arte of Prophecying on preaching, A Discourse of Conscience, and the cases of conscience. He is supralapsarian on predestination and pastoral in application, and he stands behind William Ames, much of the divinity of the Westminster men, and the Dutch Nadere Reformatie.

William Price.affiliation: Member of the Westminster Assembly; pastor of the English Reformed church at Amsterdam
William Price.bio: Welsh-born, of Christ Church, Oxford, minister at Waltham Abbey in Essex and then a member of the Westminster Assembly, where he served on committees and took part in debate. In 1648 he was called to the English Reformed congregation at Amsterdam and remained its pastor for the rest of his life. He wrote Janitor Animae (1638), a treatise on the fear of God, and Triumphus Sapientiae (Amsterdam, 1655), besides two published sermons. Reference works give his death as 1646 and as 1666, which cannot both be right, so no dates are stated here.

Wolfgang Capito.bio: Hebraist and physician who was cathedral preacher at Basel and then chancellor to the Archbishop of Mainz before joining the reform at Strasbourg in 1523, where he worked with Martin Bucer for the rest of his life. He drafted the Tetrapolitan Confession with Bucer in 1530 for the four south German cities that would not sign the Augsburg Confession, and he took part in the Wittenberg Concord of 1536. He dealt patiently with Anabaptists and spiritualists, which cost him trust on both sides, and he published Hebrew grammatical work and commentaries on Habakkuk and Hosea.

Wolfgang Franz.affiliation: Professor of theology at the University of Wittenberg
Wolfgang Franz.bio: Born at Plauen, he taught first history and then theology at Wittenberg, holding the chair until his death in 1628. His Tractatus theologicus de interpretatione sacrarum scripturarum laid down rules of scriptural interpretation for Lutheran students. His Historia animalium sacra, first printed at Wittenberg in 1612, works through the animals of the Bible, the ordinary and the legendary together, drawing a doctrinal or moral lesson from each; it was reprinted for well over a century and is the work his name is usually attached to now.

Wolfgang Musculus.bio: Lorraine-born Benedictine who left his monastery in 1527, worked as Bucer's secretary at Strasbourg, and then led the reform at Augsburg from 1531 until the Augsburg Interim drove him out in 1548. From 1549 he taught theology at Bern. He was present at the Wittenberg Concord of 1536 and at the colloquies with Catholic theologians at Worms and Regensburg. He is read for the Loci communes sacrae theologiae (1560), Englished as Common Places of Christian Religion, and for substantial commentaries on Genesis, the Psalms, Matthew, John and the Pauline letters.

Thomas Watson, Bishop of Lincoln.affiliation: Bishop of Lincoln, 1557 to 1559; Master of St John's College, Cambridge
Thomas Watson, Bishop of Lincoln.bio: A Cambridge Catholic who kept his position under Edward VI only by silence, Watson rose under Mary as chaplain and then almoner to Bishop Gardiner, Dean of Durham, and from 1557 Bishop of Lincoln. His Holsome and Catholyke Doctryne concerninge the Seven Sacramentes of 1558 is among the fullest English statements of sacramental theology printed in the Marian years. Deprived at Elizabeth's accession for refusing the oath of supremacy, he spent most of the rest of his life in custody, latterly at Wisbech Castle, and died there.

Thomas Watson (poet).affiliation: London; associated with the circle of Sir Francis Walsingham
Thomas Watson (poet).bio: Not a divine at all, and in this library by a collision of names. Watson was a lawyer by training and a poet and translator by vocation, admired by his contemporaries as a Latinist above all. The Hekatompathia of 1582 is a sequence of a hundred love poems with the author's own prose headnotes; the Lamentations of Amyntas and the Amintae Gaudia are Latin pastoral, the first Englished by Abraham Fraunce in hexameters; and the First Sett of Italian Madrigalls Englished of 1590 fitted English words to Marenzio's music. Marlowe was a friend.

Joseph Hall of Boston.bio: An American, and no relation to Joseph Hall the Bishop of Norwich, who died in 1656. The single item under this name is a civic oration delivered on 4 July 1800 at the request of a Massachusetts town and printed the same year. It is in this collection on a name match alone and belongs to a different country and a different century from everything around it.

Thomas Godwin.affiliation: Headmaster of the free school at Abingdon
Thomas Godwin.bio: A schoolmaster and antiquary, not to be confused with Thomas Goodwin the Independent divine, under whose name this work has been filed. The Romanae Historiae Anthologia of 1614 is a handbook of Roman antiquities written for schoolboys, explaining the offices, calendar, religion and customs a pupil met in Latin authors. It was reprinted many times through the century. His Moses and Aaron did the same office for Hebrew antiquities.

The Lyons editors of Albert's Opera.bio: Not Albert. The item under this name is the preface to the reader prefixed by the editors of the seventeenth-century Lyons edition of Albert's collected works, describing the edition itself rather than anything Albert wrote. It is catalogued here as though it were one of his compositions.

Thomas Goodwin the Younger.affiliation: Independent minister in London; Pinner's Hall lecturer
Thomas Goodwin the Younger.bio: Son of Thomas Goodwin the Independent, and a minister in his own right, which the catalogue does not distinguish. The two funeral sermons under this name were preached in 1695 and 1700 and cannot belong to his father, who died in 1680. He edited and saw through the press part of his father's posthumous works, which is one reason the two are so readily confused.

George Walker, Governor of Derry.affiliation: Rector of Donaghmore; joint governor of Londonderry during the siege of 1689
George Walker, Governor of Derry.bio: A clergyman of the Church of Ireland who raised a regiment and became joint governor of Londonderry through the siege of 1689, and a different man from George Walker the London Puritan controversialist, who died in 1651. His True Account of the Siege of London-Derry appeared within months and was at once disputed by John Mackenzie, which produced the Vindication also in this collection. He was killed at the Boyne in July 1690.

John Bond (pamphleteer).bio: A writer of occasional news pamphlets and verse in London in the early 1640s, and not the John Bond who preached at Exeter and sat in the Westminster Assembly, under whose name these pieces are catalogued. The five works here welcome the King home, celebrate the Parliament's return, report the fall of the old common council, and include a recantation written by a man who had stood in the pillory. Nothing further about him can be established from the catalogue.

William Ames (Quaker).affiliation: Travelling Friend in the Low Countries and the Palatinate
William Ames (Quaker).bio: A different man from William Ames the Puritan theologian of the Medulla Theologiae, who died in 1633 and under whose name these tracts have been catalogued. This Ames was among the first Friends to carry Quakerism to the Continent, working in Amsterdam and the Palatinate and disputing with the Collegiants and with Mennonites. The Light upon the Candlestick belongs to that Dutch spiritualist exchange and has also been ascribed to Pieter Balling; the Declaration of the Witness of God is a convincement narrative of the kind early Friends wrote.

Thomas Hyll.bio: An Elizabethan compiler and translator of popular science, and a different man from Thomas Hill the Westminster divine under whose name this work is catalogued. He wrote and englished cheap practical handbooks on gardening, astrology, physiognomy, dreams and household conjuring tricks, of which the Naturall and Artificiall Conclusions is one. He is in a theological library by a collision of names.

Anonymous newsbook.bio: Not an author. Two pieces of civil war ephemera, a naval report from the coast of Dunkirk and a declaration concerning Colonel John Poyer, catalogued under divines who cannot have written them: the first is dated thirteen years after John Preston died. Newsbooks of this kind were printed anonymously or under a bookseller's name, and no author can be recovered from the catalogue.

Henry Wilkinson, Sr..bio: The elder of the two Henry Wilkinsons, and father of the Magdalen Hall principal under whose name the Debt Book has been catalogued. A Puritan rector in Buckinghamshire for some fifty years, he published little; the Debt Book of 1625 is an exposition of Romans 13:8 on the duty of love as a debt owed and never discharged.

Captain Henry Wilkinson.bio: Not a divine. The single item under this name is a printed information, that is a sworn deposition, laid during the Popish Plot years and concerning what had passed between the deponent and others. It is catalogued with the sermons of Henry Wilkinson the Oxford divine on a shared name.
